prompt: A collegiate sprinter explodes from the blocks and covers the opening six seconds of a short dash at maximal effort. Which energy system supplies most of the ATP for that burst?

options.text: The phosphagen ATP-PC system supplies most of the ATP for this brief sprint.
Aerobic fat oxidation supplies most of the ATP once those six seconds are underway.
Fast glycolysis supplies most of the ATP across a maximal sprint this short.
Blood glucose taken up during the sprint covers nearly the entire ATP cost of the burst.

explanation: A maximal effort of about six seconds draws most of its ATP from stored ATP and phosphocreatine, the phosphagen system. Glycolysis contributes, but it is not the main supplier yet, and fat oxidation is too slow for this opening burst.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses this six-second sprint with aerobic fat oxidation, which cannot supply most of the ATP on that time scale.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the phosphagen system with fast glycolysis, which contributes but does not supply most of the ATP in six seconds.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses muscle phosphagens with blood glucose delivery, which is too slow to be the main ATP source in the first six seconds.

prompt: Before loading a heavy Olympic pull, the coach asks which fiber type can shorten fastest and produce the greatest power. Which fiber should she favor for peak bar speed?

options.text: Type I fibers, the oxidative fibers with the greatest power on this heavy pull.
Type IIx fibers, which shorten fastest and hold the highest power potential.
Type IIa fibers, the longer-lasting fibers with more power than Type IIx fibers.
Hybrid fibers, which shorten faster and produce more power than Type IIx fibers.

explanation: Type IIx fibers have the fastest myosin ATPase activity and the highest power output, so they are the fibers to favor when the pull needs peak shortening speed. Type I fibers are built for endurance, and Type IIa fibers sit between those extremes.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses Type I oxidative endurance fibers with the fast, high-power Type IIx fibers this pull needs for bar speed.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses Type IIa fatigue resistance with the greater shortening speed and power of Type IIx fibers.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats hybrid fibers as the powerful option and misses that Type IIx fibers themselves have the highest power potential.

prompt: Across the first three weeks of bench training, a novice adds load every session while upper-arm girth barely changes. What most likely explains those rapid early strength gains?

options.text: A large jump in muscle cross-sectional area that a tape measure would fail to catch.
Conversion of slow fibers into fast fibers across those first few bench sessions.
Improved motor-unit recruitment, firing rate, and coordination of the press.
A sharp rise in stored muscle glycogen that directly lifts one-repetition bench strength.

explanation: Strength can jump in the first weeks before measurable hypertrophy. The nervous system recruits more motor units, fires them faster, and coordinates the press, which matches a bigger load with almost no change in arm girth.

distractorExplanations.a: Mistakes early strength for hypertrophy, but arm girth barely changed, so a large rise in muscle size is not what happened.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses neural learning with fiber-type conversion, which does not account for a strength jump over three weeks of benching.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a neural strength gain with extra stored glycogen, which does not by itself raise one-repetition bench strength.

prompt: Driving a barbell from the hole of a back squat up toward standing, this athlete's knees straighten under the load. What action are the knee extensors performing during that ascent?

options.text: An isometric action, because knee angle stays fixed once the bar leaves the bottom.
A lengthening action, because the rising bar is what stretches the quadriceps.
A passive recoil, because the knee extensors stop producing force as the bar rises.
A concentric action, because those knee extensors shorten as the knees extend.

explanation: On the way up, the quadriceps produce force while shortening to extend the knees. Shortening under load is a concentric action. The knees are opening, so this ascent is not a fixed hold or a passive rise.

distractorExplanations.a: Calls the ascent isometric, but the knees are straightening, so the joint angle is changing rather than holding still.
distractorExplanations.b: Claims the rising bar stretches the quadriceps, but on the way up those knee extensors are shortening, not lengthening.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the rise as passive recoil and misses that the knee extensors are actively shortening against the load.

prompt: A basketball player dips quickly and then leaves the floor on a countermovement jump during a layup drill. Which sequence of muscle actions makes up that stretch-shortening cycle?

options.text: An eccentric dip, a brief amortization phase, then a concentric takeoff.
A long pause in the bottom, then a fixed hold that drives her off the floor.
Three shortening pulses, with no lengthening of the leg muscles before takeoff.
A shortening preload first, followed by a slow lowering after she has landed.

explanation: The stretch-shortening cycle uses a quick eccentric dip, a brief amortization, and then a concentric takeoff, so elastic energy and the reflex can add to the jump. A long pause, shortening-only pulses, or saving the lengthening for the landing is a different pattern.

distractorExplanations.b: Replaces the quick eccentric-to-concentric transition with a long pause and a fixed hold, which is not the stretch-shortening cycle.
distractorExplanations.c: Drops the eccentric dip and calls the jump shortening-only pulses, so the stretch phase is missing.
distractorExplanations.d: Reverses the order by starting with shortening and saving the lengthening phase for after the landing.

prompt: After ten weeks of steady running, imaging shows a distance athlete sending out more blood with each beat at rest and on easy miles. Which cardiovascular adaptation is that?

options.text: A higher maximal heart rate as the main change earned from those easy miles.
Increased stroke volume at rest and during submaximal exercise bouts.
A smaller left ventricle that ejects less blood with each beat at rest.
A loss of blood volume so each beat moves less blood on those easy miles.

explanation: Endurance training commonly increases stroke volume, the blood ejected each beat, both at rest and during submaximal work such as easy miles. That is the adaptation the imaging shows. A higher maximal heart rate is not the usual endurance change.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a larger stroke volume with a higher maximal heart rate, which is not the usual adaptation to endurance training.
distractorExplanations.c: Reverses the finding and describes a smaller ventricle ejecting less blood, the opposite of what the imaging shows.
distractorExplanations.d: Describes a loss of blood volume and less blood per beat, which contradicts sending more blood out with each beat.

prompt: In an exercise laboratory, a rower stays on a rowing ergometer after oxygen uptake has stopped rising even as the flywheel drag increases. What does that peak oxygen-uptake value represent?

options.text: The oxygen cost of sitting quietly on the ergometer before the test starts.
Oxygen stored in the lungs, with muscular use of oxygen left out of the value.
The highest rate at which oxygen can be taken up and used in hard work.
The stage where lactate first rises, whether or not oxygen uptake has peaked.

explanation: VO2max is the highest rate at which oxygen can be taken up and used during intense exercise. A plateau while flywheel drag still rises is how the lab marks that ceiling. It is not the resting cost, lung storage alone, or the first lactate rise.

distractorExplanations.a: Substitutes the resting oxygen cost on the ergometer for the peak rate reached in hard work.
distractorExplanations.b: Limits the value to oxygen stored in the lungs and leaves out muscular use, which this peak includes.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the highest oxygen-uptake rate with the first lactate rise, which can occur before oxygen uptake peaks.

prompt: A model sarcomere has already shortened so far that the thin filaments overlap each other, and active force falls. Why does force decline at that extremely short length?

options.text: Cross-bridge overlap keeps improving as the sarcomere shortens, so force should have risen.
Calcium can no longer bind troponin once the sarcomere is shorter than resting length.
The tendon absorbs the shortening, so this sarcomere itself produces no active force.
Actin filaments overlap and interfere, cutting effective cross-bridge force.

explanation: At an extremely short sarcomere length, the thin filaments overlap and interfere with each other, so fewer cross-bridges can pull effectively and force falls. Useful force needs favorable overlap, not the most shortened position the model can reach.

distractorExplanations.a: Expects force to rise as overlap improves with shortening, and misses the interference that cuts force at an extremely short length.
distractorExplanations.b: Blames failed calcium-troponin binding below resting length, which is not why force falls once the thin filaments overlap.
distractorExplanations.c: Moves the force loss into the tendon and misses actin overlap interfering with cross-bridges inside the short sarcomere.

prompt: During a maximal isometric leg-press hold, tension rises sharply where the quadriceps tendon meets the patella. Which proprioceptor is specialized to sense that high muscle tension?

options.text: The Golgi tendon organ, which senses tension at the musculotendinous junction.
A joint-capsule receptor that mainly reports knee angle rather than tendon tension.
A vibration-sensitive skin corpuscle that tracks shaking rather than tendon load.
A free nerve ending that reports muscle ache rather than tension in the tendon.

explanation: Golgi tendon organs sit near the musculotendinous junction and respond to tension. A hard isometric leg-press hold raises tension in the quadriceps tendon, so that organ is the receptor built for this signal. Joint angle, skin vibration, and muscle ache are different senses.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a joint-capsule angle receptor with the Golgi tendon organ, which monitors tension rather than knee position.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a skin vibration receptor with the tendon organ that senses muscle tension during the hold.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a pain-sensing free nerve ending with the Golgi tendon organ, which monitors tension during the hold.

prompt: Stepping straight forward, an athlete flexes and then extends the hip and knee through a forward lunge. In which plane does that main motion occur, and about which axis?

options.text: Transverse-plane trunk rotation about a vertical longitudinal axis.
Sagittal-plane flexion and extension about a mediolateral axis.
Sagittal-plane flexion and extension about a vertical axis.
Frontal-plane side bending about a vertical axis through the hip.

explanation: A forward lunge's main hip and knee flexion and extension travel in the sagittal plane and rotate about a mediolateral axis. Trunk twisting about a vertical axis, or side bending, is not the dominant action of this forward step.

distractorExplanations.a: Assigns transverse-plane rotation about a vertical axis, but the step is forward flexion and extension, not a twist.
distractorExplanations.c: Keeps the sagittal plane but swaps in a vertical axis, which is the wrong axis for flexion and extension.
distractorExplanations.d: Moves the forward lunge into frontal-plane side bending about a vertical axis, which is not this step.

prompt: Halfway down the homestretch of a one-lap race, glycolytic flux is high and her working legs cannot clear lactate as fast as it forms. What happens to lactate?

options.text: It is cleared in the same moment it forms, so the blood level stays flat.
Formation stops as soon as breathing quickens, so no extra lactate remains.
Lactate accumulates in the blood and in the working muscles of both legs.
It is cleared from the muscle and destroyed in the blood, so the muscle level falls.

explanation: When glycolytic production of lactate outruns clearance, lactate accumulates in the working muscle and in the blood. Faster breathing does not stop that buildup, and lactate is not cleared out of the muscle so that the muscle level falls.

distractorExplanations.a: Assumes clearance matches production in the same moment, but this is the case where clearance has already fallen behind.
distractorExplanations.b: Thinks faster breathing shuts off lactate formation, which does not stop accumulation while glycolytic flux stays high.
distractorExplanations.d: Says muscle lactate falls because the blood destroys it, but production above clearance makes lactate accumulate in muscle and blood.

prompt: Two hours into a long steady ride, a cyclist's fuel mobilization rises and muscle protein breakdown ticks upward. Which hormone plays that acute catabolic role during prolonged exercise?

options.text: Insulin, which surges during a long hard ride and builds new muscle.
Testosterone, the hormone that breaks muscle protein down on this long ride.
Glucagon, the acute catabolic hormone, because it frees stored fuel on the ride.
Cortisol, which plays the acute catabolic role during prolonged exercise.

explanation: During prolonged exercise, cortisol supports fuel mobilization and protein breakdown, so it is the acute catabolic hormone in this long ride. Insulin does not surge to build muscle here, and testosterone and glucagon are not that catabolic driver.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses cortisol's catabolic, fuel-mobilizing role with insulin, which does not surge to build muscle during a long hard ride.
distractorExplanations.b: Swaps cortisol for testosterone, an anabolic hormone, and misses cortisol's acute catabolic role in prolonged exercise.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses glucagon's fuel-mobilizing role with cortisol, the acute catabolic hormone during prolonged exercise.

prompt: A lifter starts with a light dumbbell curl and adds plates until the final reps approach failure. In what order are motor units generally recruited as the force demand climbs?

options.text: From smaller, low-threshold units first toward larger, high-threshold units.
From the largest, fastest units first, saving small units until fatigue sets in.
In a shuffled order that changes every rep and follows no threshold pattern.
High-threshold units on the light load, then low-threshold units near failure.

explanation: The size principle generally recruits smaller, low-threshold motor units first and adds larger, high-threshold units as force demand rises. The light curl starts with low-threshold units, and heavier reps bring in larger ones. The order does not flip as the weight goes up.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses the size principle by recruiting the largest units first and saving small units for fatigue.
distractorExplanations.c: Replaces orderly low-to-high recruitment with a shuffled pattern that the size principle does not describe.
distractorExplanations.d: Flips the order, putting high-threshold units on the light load and low-threshold units near failure.

prompt: After skipping fluids through a hot afternoon practice, a soccer player repeats yesterday's shuttle pace and feels the same work hit harder. How does that dehydration change cardiovascular strain?

options.text: It expands plasma volume, so heart rate falls at the same shuttle pace.
It lowers plasma volume and raises heart rate for that same workload.
It leaves plasma volume unchanged and merely slows her breathing rate.
Heart rate rises from a higher oxygen demand, while plasma volume stays the same.

explanation: Dehydration lowers plasma volume, so heart rate rises to support the same shuttle pace. That pairing is the higher cardiovascular strain at a given workload. Skipped fluids in the heat do not expand plasma volume or leave it untouched.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses both effects, claiming plasma volume rises and heart rate falls, the opposite of this dehydration.
distractorExplanations.c: Denies the drop in plasma volume and relocates the change to a slower breathing rate.
distractorExplanations.d: Raises heart rate for a metabolic reason and holds plasma volume constant, missing the volume loss that drives the strain.

prompt: Gripping the same dumbbell force, a lifter lets the forearm drift so the weight sits farther from the elbow joint. Which change raises torque at the elbow if the force stays constant?

options.text: Shortening the perpendicular moment arm while the dumbbell force stays the same.
Placing the load on the elbow axis so the moment arm falls away to nothing.
Lengthening the perpendicular moment arm from the elbow axis to the load.
Speeding the curl up while leaving the perpendicular distance from the axis unchanged.

explanation: Torque equals force times the perpendicular moment arm. With dumbbell force held constant, a weight sitting farther from the elbow lengthens that moment arm and raises torque. Shortening the arm, putting the load on the axis, or speeding the curl without a longer arm does not.

distractorExplanations.a: Shortens the moment arm, which would lower torque if force stays the same, the opposite of this farther load.
distractorExplanations.b: Puts the load on the joint axis and removes the moment arm, so torque falls rather than rises.
distractorExplanations.d: Changes curl speed and leaves the perpendicular moment arm alone, so torque at constant force does not rise.

prompt: A clinician taps just below the kneecap, and the lower leg kicks forward in a reflex before the athlete decides to move. Which receptor detected that sudden stretch?

options.text: The muscle spindle, which responds to a quick stretch of the thigh.
The Golgi tendon organ, reading the tendon tap as rising tension rather than a sudden stretch.
A pressure receptor in the kneecap that times the kick without sensing stretch in the thigh.
A joint receptor that reports the new knee angle rather than the quick stretch.

explanation: The tap quickly stretches the quadriceps, and the muscle spindle responds to that stretch to trigger the knee jerk. The Golgi tendon organ senses tension, not this sudden length change. Kneecap pressure and a joint-angle signal are not the stretch receptor.

distractorExplanations.b: Assigns the knee jerk to the Golgi tendon organ, which senses tension, and misses the muscle spindle's response to quick stretch.
distractorExplanations.c: Substitutes a kneecap pressure receptor for the muscle spindle that detects the sudden stretch of the thigh.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a joint-angle receptor with the muscle spindle, which responds to the quick stretch of the tap.

prompt: Each morning across eight weeks of easy aerobic miles, a runner checks her pulse while still lying quietly in bed. What resting heart-rate change should follow that endurance block?

options.text: Resting heart rate climbs, because easy miles force the heart to beat faster even during sleep.
The morning resting heart rate falls after those weeks of endurance work.
Resting heart rate stays locked at the week-one value, because easy miles leave a morning pulse unchanged.
Resting heart rate turns irregular and faster, taken as the expected mark of aerobic fitness.

explanation: Weeks of aerobic work commonly slow the morning resting heart rate. The coach should expect that in-bed pulse to fall. A faster, frozen, or irregular resting rate is not the usual endurance change in heart rate at rest.

distractorExplanations.a: Predicts a faster sleeping heart rate, but endurance work usually lowers resting heart rate rather than raising it.
distractorExplanations.c: Claims easy aerobic miles leave the morning pulse unchanged, missing the usual drop in resting heart rate.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a faster, irregular pulse as fitness, which is not the resting heart-rate change endurance training produces.

prompt: A throws coach tells a shot-putter to rely on Type I fibers for one all-out put. What is true of Type I fibers in that single maximal throw?

options.text: They are the fastest fibers in the muscle and the right choice for one all-out put.
Their dense mitochondria make them the best fiber choice for a single maximal throw.
They are fatigue-resistant and slower, a poor match for this throw.
They convert into fast fibers for the put, then convert back before the next attempt.

explanation: Type I fibers are fatigue-resistant and slower, so they are a poor match for one maximal shot put, which needs high shortening speed and power. Mitochondrial density does not make them the throwing fiber, and they do not switch fiber type for a single attempt.

distractorExplanations.a: Calls Type I fibers the fastest and the right choice for a maximal put, which reverses their slower, fatigue-resistant profile.
distractorExplanations.b: Treats mitochondrial density as a reason to pick Type I fibers for one maximal throw, missing that they are slower.
distractorExplanations.d: Invents a fiber-type conversion for one put instead of recognizing that Type I fibers stay slower and fatigue-resistant.

prompt: Between two maximal forty-meter repeats, a sprinter allows only the ten-second walk back to the start line. How long does meaningful phosphagen recovery between those repeats actually take?

options.text: A ten-second walk-back fully restores phosphagen stores before the next maximal repeat.
Phosphagen stores are restored before the athlete finishes turning around at the start line.
Phosphagen stores stay depleted until the next day, so repeats in the same session cannot recover.
Recovery takes rest on the order of minutes, not a ten-second pause.

explanation: Meaningful recovery of the phosphagen pool between maximal repeats takes rest on the order of minutes. A ten-second walk-back is too short. Turning around does not refill the pool, and recovery is not pushed out until the next day.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a ten-second pause as full phosphagen recovery, but meaningful recovery between maximal repeats takes minutes.
distractorExplanations.b: Compresses phosphagen recovery into the time it takes to turn around, far shorter than rest on the order of minutes.
distractorExplanations.c: Pushes recovery to the next day and misses that minutes of rest, not a full day, restore the pool between repeats.

prompt: Stretched until its sarcomeres are extremely long, a single muscle fiber produces less active force than it did near resting length. Why does force drop at that very long length?

options.text: Fewer cross-bridges overlap the thin filament, so active force falls.
Thin filaments collide and block one another, the problem seen when a sarcomere is extremely short.
Passive structures go slack at this long length, and that slack is why active force fell.
Actin and myosin overlap more at this long length, so active force should have gone up.

explanation: At a very long sarcomere length, actin and myosin overlap less, so fewer cross-bridges can form and active force drops. That is the long-length end of the curve. Filaments colliding is the short-length problem, and overlap does not increase here.

distractorExplanations.b: Imports the extremely short sarcomere problem, filaments blocking one another, into a long length where overlap is reduced.
distractorExplanations.c: Blames slack passive structures, but at a very long length the active-force loss is fewer overlapping cross-bridges.
distractorExplanations.d: Expects more filament overlap and higher force at a long length, the opposite of the reduced overlap here.

prompt: Midway through a hard set of leg presses, cardiac output is elevated and the coach asks which tissues receive the extra blood. Where is that added flow directed?

options.text: Toward the gut and the kidneys, with less blood reaching the muscles that are pressing.
More blood flow to the working legs, not more flow to the gut.
Toward the skin of the face, with leg-muscle flow left unchanged through the whole set.
Toward the resting arms, while the working legs lose blood flow during the set.

explanation: During a hard leg-press set, more of the cardiac output goes to the working leg muscles, and flow there rises. Flow to the gut does not rise with it. Facial skin and resting arms are not where that added flow is directed.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the redistribution, sending the extra cardiac output to the gut and kidneys instead of the working legs.
distractorExplanations.c: Parks the extra flow in facial skin and denies the rise in blood flow to the muscles doing the press.
distractorExplanations.d: Sends blood toward inactive arms and takes flow from the working legs, the opposite of where output is directed.

prompt: Choosing words for approach jumps that a volleyball player already performs well, the coach weighs a floor-target phrase against a thigh-muscle phrase. Which cue should aid that well-learned jump more?

options.text: An internal cue to squeeze the quadriceps, preferred once a jump is already well learned.
A cue asking him to watch the thigh muscle contract, because body-focused words sharpen a skill he owns.
Push the floor away, an external cue, rather than squeeze the quad.
Neither phrase, because wording aimed outside the body will disrupt a jump he already performs well.

explanation: For a jump he already knows, an external cue such as push the floor away supports performance better than an internal cue such as squeeze the quad. Attention on the effect of the jump beats attention on the muscle.

distractorExplanations.a: Prefers the internal cue to squeeze the quadriceps, which is the weaker cue once the jump is already well learned.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses a body-focused cue about watching the thigh contract, an internal focus, instead of an external floor cue.
distractorExplanations.d: Rejects an outside-the-body phrase, but that external cue is the one that should help this well-learned jump more.

prompt: Monday is squat-only, Wednesday is press-only, and Friday is pull-only, and each blocked day feels smooth. For transfer of those same three lifts into sport, which schedule works better?

options.text: Blocked practice transfers better, because the smooth feeling that day predicts carryover into sport.
A full month of squat work by itself transfers better than mixing the three lifts in one session.
A personality score should pick the schedule, because the order of the lifts does not change transfer.
Random practice of the three lifts transfers better to the sport.

explanation: Blocked practice often feels smoother that day, but random practice of the same three lifts transfers better to the mixed demands of sport. How Monday felt is that day's performance. A personality score does not choose the schedule.

distractorExplanations.a: Judges sport transfer by how smooth the blocked day felt, which tracks that session rather than carryover.
distractorExplanations.b: Extends single-lift work for a month and misses that mixing the three lifts in random order transfers better.
distractorExplanations.c: Turns a practice-schedule choice into a personality score, which does not decide how these lifts transfer.

prompt: Mid-set, an athlete becomes breathless, says she thinks she is having a panic attack, and cannot finish the lift. What should the strength and conditioning coach do next?

options.text: Stop the session and refer; a coach does not diagnose the attack.
Finish the remaining repetitions, then lead a breathing script as though diagnosing the attack.
Record a panic disorder on the workout card and write a home treatment plan for tonight.
Add a heavier set, treating the report as a focus lapse that more load will solve.

explanation: A strength and conditioning coach does not diagnose a panic attack. The session stops, and the athlete is referred. Finishing the set, labeling a disorder, or adding load is outside that role.

distractorExplanations.b: Keeps the set going and has the coach run a diagnostic breathing script, which is not the coach's job.
distractorExplanations.c: Has the coach label a panic disorder and assign a home plan, which a strength coach does not diagnose or prescribe.
distractorExplanations.d: Dismisses the report as a focus lapse and adds load instead of stopping the session and referring.

prompt: Seeing a lower absolute squat from a female lifter than from a male teammate, a coach wonders if her motor units recruit in reverse. What stays the same between them?

options.text: The lifter with the lighter squat recruits large high-threshold units first.
Recruitment order does not reverse, even if absolute strength differs.
The heavier squatter skips low-threshold units, so low-to-high order is not shared.
A lower absolute squat means recruitment runs backward in the lifter who squats less.

explanation: Low-threshold motor units are recruited before high-threshold units in female and male athletes alike. Absolute strength can differ without reversing that order. A lighter squat is not evidence that recruitment runs backward.

distractorExplanations.a: Claims the lighter squatter recruits high-threshold units first, but a strength difference does not reverse recruitment order.
distractorExplanations.c: Claims the heavier squatter skips low-threshold units, but both lifters follow the same low-to-high order.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a difference in absolute squat strength as proof that recruitment order flips, which it does not.

prompt: In the first days of a high-elevation camp, a distance runner keeps a sea-level pace she can still sustain and asks her coach why that pace feels harder. What change in oxygen uptake explains the harder effort?

options.text: Lactate disappears at this elevation, so the harder effort is not an oxygen-uptake problem.
Oxygen uptake at this pace climbs above the maximum she could reach at sea level.
Maximal oxygen uptake is lower, so this pace takes a larger share of it.
Less oxygen is taken up at this same pace than at sea level, and that shortfall is why the effort is harder.

explanation: During the first week at elevation, maximal oxygen uptake falls because each breath and each liter of blood carry less oxygen. A pace she can still hold costs about the same oxygen as at sea level, so that pace is a larger share of a lower ceiling and feels harder. Lactate does not disappear, and uptake at the pace does not climb above her sea-level maximum.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the first-week altitude effect with lactate disappearing, but lactate does not vanish and that idea does not explain why the pace feels harder.
distractorExplanations.b: Claims oxygen uptake at this pace exceeds her sea-level maximum, but the first week at elevation lowers that ceiling instead of raising uptake at the pace.
distractorExplanations.d: Treats a drop in oxygen uptake at the same pace as the reason the effort is harder, but a pace she can still hold costs about the same oxygen; maximal uptake is what falls.

prompt: Controlling a heavy descent, she lets the hips and knees fold as the bar sinks. Which muscle action best describes the quadriceps on this lowering phase?

options.text: Shortening while the bar rises, with this lowering phase treated as the same pattern.
A fixed-length hold, because the quadriceps freeze the knee while the bar sinks.
No muscular action, because the quadriceps switch off for the entire lowering phase.
An eccentric action: the knee extensors lengthen under load on the way down.

explanation: As the bar sinks and the knees bend, the knee extensors produce force while they lengthen. That lowering phase is an eccentric action. It is not the shortening pattern of the ascent, a fixed knee angle, or a muscle that has switched off.

distractorExplanations.a: Applies the shortening pattern of the ascent to this lowering phase, where the knee extensors are lengthening under load.
distractorExplanations.b: Calls the descent a fixed-length hold, but the knees are folding, so the quadriceps are not staying at one length.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats a controlled descent as a switched-off muscle, missing the eccentric force as the knee extensors lengthen.

prompt: A sport scientist reminds a sprinter that the ATP already sitting inside the muscle covers only a brief instant of maximal effort. What rebuilds that very small immediate pool?

options.text: The phosphagen system rebuilds that very small immediate ATP pool.
Fat oxidation rebuilds ATP fast enough to carry a few seconds of maximal sprinting.
A large stock of muscle ATP covers minutes of maximal work, so nothing has to rebuild it.
Lactate stored in the fiber is the high-energy pool that directly replaces the used ATP.

explanation: Muscle holds only a very small immediate ATP pool, enough for a brief instant of maximal work. The phosphagen system rapidly rebuilds that ATP. Fat oxidation is not the rebuild pathway for a few seconds of sprinting, and lactate is not a stored ATP substitute.

distractorExplanations.b: Makes fat oxidation the pathway that rebuilds ATP for a few seconds of maximal sprinting, which is too slow for that job.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats stored ATP as a minutes-long tank, missing how small the immediate pool is and that the phosphagen system rebuilds it.
distractorExplanations.d: Substitutes stored lactate for the phosphagen system as the pool that directly replaces ATP.

prompt: From a narrow stance she steps directly sideways into a lateral lunge, then pushes back to standing. Which plane contains the main motion of that side step?

options.text: The sagittal plane, because a step to the side is still scored as a forward hip hinge.
The transverse plane, because stepping sideways is rotation and not a frontal-plane motion.
No cardinal plane, because a wider base is balance practice and not a joint motion.
The main motion is in the frontal plane about an anteroposterior axis.

explanation: A lateral lunge steps to the side, so the main hip motion is in the frontal plane about an anteroposterior axis. A wider base does change balance, but the side step is still frontal-plane motion, not a forward hinge or pure rotation.

distractorExplanations.a: Calls the side step a sagittal hip hinge, which describes a forward step rather than this lateral lunge.
distractorExplanations.b: Reduces the lateral lunge to transverse rotation and denies the frontal-plane motion of the side step.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the wider base as balance with no plane, missing that the side step itself is frontal-plane motion.

prompt: Late in a graded cycling test, stroke volume has leveled off while heart rate is still climbing toward its maximum. How can cardiac output keep rising?

options.text: Through a late surge in stroke volume that appears as heart rate reaches its maximum.
It cannot keep rising once stroke volume levels off, even while heart rate is still climbing.
Through a drop in heart rate, which is what lifts cardiac output at the end of this test.
Heart rate is still climbing, so cardiac output can keep rising.

explanation: Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume. After stroke volume levels off, a heart rate that is still climbing can keep cardiac output rising. Output does not need a second surge in stroke volume, and it does not rise by slowing the heart.

distractorExplanations.a: Requires another rise in stroke volume near max heart rate, but output can keep rising through the heart rate that is still climbing.
distractorExplanations.b: Claims cardiac output must stop once stroke volume levels off, ignoring the heart-rate rise that can still lift output.
distractorExplanations.c: Lowers heart rate to raise cardiac output, which reverses how output can keep rising near the end of the test.

prompt: A collegiate sprinter finishes a set of 200-meter repeats and asks which fuel her muscles relied on most while those hard efforts stayed fast rather than easy jogging?

options.text: Carbohydrate supplied by muscle glycogen and blood glucose.
Fat supplied by intramuscular triglyceride during the repeats.
Amino acids stripped from muscle to run those fast repeats.
Phosphocreatine alone, with carbohydrate left out of the work.

explanation: Repeats this fast and long draw on glycolysis, which runs on muscle glycogen and blood glucose. Fat oxidation can dominate easy jogging, but it is too slow to be the main supply while she stays at 200-meter pace. Protein is not the fuel for that work.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the fuel for easy aerobic jogging with the fuel for fast glycolytic repeats. Intramuscular fat is not the main supply at this pace.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses tissue breakdown with a fuel source. Amino acids are not what glycolysis uses to cover a set of 200-meter repeats.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the shortest explosive efforts with these longer repeats. Leaving carbohydrate out misses the fuel the glycolytic work actually uses.

prompt: A linebacker checks a whey-isolate label that lists the protein in grams and wants the energy those grams contribute, ignoring the brand's marketing claims about recovery?

options.text: About 9 kilocalories, which is the yield that belongs to fat.
About 4 kilocalories for each gram of protein on that label.
No usable kilocalories, because protein is kept for tissue repair.
About 4 kilocalories per ounce, mixing up the unit on the label.

explanation: Protein contributes about 4 kilocalories per gram, the same energy density as carbohydrate. The linebacker should multiply the grams on the whey label by about 4. Fat is the macronutrient at about 9, and protein is not a zero-energy food just because it also supports tissue.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses protein with fat. About 9 kilocalories per gram is the fat figure, not the whey protein he is reading.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a building role with zero energy. Protein still supplies about 4 kilocalories per gram when those grams are eaten.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses the unit. The 4 kilocalorie figure is per gram, not per ounce, so the label's gram line is the one that counts.

prompt: After a two-hour soccer match empties the midfielder's glycogen, the coach asks what carbohydrate at the next meal is mainly there to do?

options.text: To drive overnight fat use instead of putting carbohydrate back.
To replace the sodium the midfielder lost in match sweat.
To speed muscle glycogen resynthesis after that depleting match.
To rebuild phosphocreatine, a store carbohydrate does not refill.

explanation: A match long enough to empty muscle glycogen is followed by carbohydrate so resynthesis can speed up. The next meal's carbohydrate supplies glucose for that refill. It is not a fat-burning trick, a sodium replacement, or the way phosphocreatine is restored.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses glycogen restoration with a fat-oxidation goal. Carbohydrate after a depleting match refills glycogen rather than driving overnight fat use.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses carbohydrate with an electrolyte. Sodium replaces sweat sodium; it is not what this post-match carbohydrate feeding is for.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses glycogen with phosphocreatine. Carbohydrate after the match speeds glycogen resynthesis and does not rebuild the phosphocreatine store.

prompt: Three hours before tipoff, a point guard is choosing dinner and needs a meal pattern that will fuel the game without sitting heavy. Which plate fits?

options.text: An unfamiliar high-fiber chili he has not tried before a game.
A large fried cheese platter eaten in the last stretch before tipoff.
A protein-heavy plate that leaves carbohydrate off the dinner menu.
A familiar carb-rich plate, moderate protein, little fat or fiber.

explanation: Three hours out sits in the two-to-four-hour window. The plate that fits is one he already tolerates, rich in carbohydrate, with moderate protein and not much fat or fiber, so fuel is available without a heavy stomach. New fiber, a greasy fry, or a near-zero carbohydrate dinner misses that pattern.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses novelty with a safe pregame plate. An unfamiliar high-fiber chili is a gastrointestinal risk, not the familiar meal this window calls for.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a heavy fried plate with pregame fuel. Extra fat and cheese this close to tipoff sit in the stomach instead of providing an easy carbohydrate supply.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a protein-only dinner with game fuel. Leaving carbohydrate off the plate under-fuels the work the guard is about to play.

prompt: A football lineman finishes a humid August practice soaked through, and the staff wants the main performance problem created by that heavy sweat loss?

options.text: Weaker cooling together with a higher cardiovascular strain.
Little performance cost, because he did not feel thirsty in practice.
Lost muscle equal to the sweat, as if jersey fluid were lean tissue.
Better sprint power from the lighter body after that sweat loss.

explanation: A large sweat loss lowers plasma volume. The lineman then has a harder time dissipating heat, and the cardiovascular system works harder for a given effort. That combination, not a hidden performance benefit, is the main problem the staff should name.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the absence of thirst with no cost. Heavy sweat loss still impairs cooling and raises cardiovascular strain whether or not he noticed thirst.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses sweat on the jersey with lost muscle. The fluid is not lean tissue, and the performance problem is cooling plus cardiovascular strain.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a lighter scale with better power. The sweat loss impairs thermoregulation and raises cardiovascular strain rather than improving his sprinting.

prompt: A powerlifter eats nearly all of his daily protein in one late plate and asks whether splitting that same total across breakfast, lunch, and dinner changes muscle building?

options.text: One late plate builds more muscle than splitting those same grams across meals.
Repeated protein feedings support muscle-protein synthesis across the day.
The split is really there to speed glycogen resynthesis, not muscle.
Skipping breakfast raises synthesis by letting the gut stay empty.

explanation: Spreading the same protein across breakfast, lunch, and dinner gives repeated rises in amino acids that support muscle-protein synthesis through the day. Parking nearly all of it on one late plate misses those earlier feedings. The split is about muscle protein, not glycogen, and skipping breakfast does not help.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses one large bolus with a better muscle-building pattern. The same grams support synthesis better when they are repeated across meals.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses protein distribution with carbohydrate recovery. Speeding glycogen resynthesis is a carbohydrate job, not why this protein is split.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an empty stretch with a synthesis benefit. Skipping breakfast removes a feeding that would have supported muscle-protein synthesis.

prompt: A strength coach is asked which researched supplement most reliably helps athletes repeat heavy lifts and short all-out efforts, among products sold at the gym counter?

options.text: An iron tablet started on a hunch for lifters who feel tired.
A detox tea marketed to drop scale weight before a weigh-in.
Creatine monohydrate for repeated hard efforts and heavy lifting.
A doubled coffee taken the morning of competition, past usual habit.

explanation: Creatine monohydrate has the strong evidence for repeated high-intensity work and strength. It raises muscle phosphocreatine so rapid ATP regeneration can continue across those efforts. An iron hunch, a detox tea, and a doubled game-morning coffee are not that supplement.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a guessed iron tablet with an evidence-backed performance supplement. Iron is not the product with strong support for repeated lifts and all-out efforts.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a weight-cut tea with performance support. A detox product marketed for the scale does not have this evidence for strength and repeated hard work.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a last-minute caffeine jump with the researched choice. Doubling coffee past habit is not the supplement that reliably supports these efforts.

prompt: During a three-hour tennis match in full sun, a player asks what dietary sodium adds beyond the water she is already drinking from the bottle?

options.text: It stands in for the carbohydrate used across a long hot match.
It pulls water out of the body, so it is best avoided in the sun.
It behaves like a stimulant, in the same way a strong coffee does.
It replaces sodium lost in sweat and helps the body hold fluid.

explanation: A long match in the sun produces a large sweat loss that carries sodium. Replacing that sodium helps the player retain the fluid she drinks, which water alone does not do as well. Sodium is not a substitute for carbohydrate, a reason to avoid fluid, or a stimulant.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses sodium with match fuel. Carbohydrate covers the energy cost; sodium's role here is replacing sweat sodium and helping hold fluid.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses sodium with a dehydrating agent. In this long sweaty match, sodium supports fluid retention rather than pulling water out.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses sodium with caffeine. Sodium does not act as a stimulant; it replaces sweat losses and helps the body keep fluid.

prompt: A wrestler plans to drop a weight class before Friday's weigh-in by skipping meals and sitting in a sauna. What does that crash cut typically cost?

options.text: Lean mass, recovery, health, and how he performs in competition.
Water on the scale, with strength and skill left fully intact.
Body fat by itself, cleared on a timetable of a few days.
Nothing that matters, because making the scale is the whole goal.

explanation: Skipping meals and sweating off a weight class in a few days is a rapid cut. That pattern costs lean mass, recovery, health, and performance, even if Friday's scale looks successful. It does not peel off fat alone or leave strength and skill untouched.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a rapid cut with harmless water loss. Strength, skill, recovery, and lean mass are not left intact by skipping meals and a sauna.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a crash cut with selective fat loss. A few days of starvation and sauna do not clear body fat by itself.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses making weight with a cost-free goal. The scale drop still sacrifices lean mass, recovery, health, and performance.

prompt: A distance runner's log shows she eats far less than she burns in training. Which description matches the energy-availability figure the sport dietitian is calculating?

options.text: The kilocalories in the sports drink she uses on the run.
Dietary energy left for normal physiology after the training cost.
The scale drop that appears when glycogen and water leave together.
The protein grams that turn directly into new muscle tissue.

explanation: Energy availability is the dietary energy left for normal physiological function once the cost of exercise is subtracted. Her log shows intake far below training expenditure, so that leftover figure is what the dietitian is naming. It is not the sports drink alone, a scale change, or protein turning into muscle.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses energy availability with one bottle during the run. The figure is dietary energy remaining after exercise cost, not the drink by itself.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses energy availability with a quick scale change. Glycogen and water leaving together move weight; they are not the leftover energy for physiology.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses energy availability with muscle building. Protein grams are not the energy left for normal body functions after training.

prompt: A cross-country athlete asks which mineral sits inside hemoglobin so red blood cells can carry oxygen to working muscle during races?

options.text: Sodium, which some people picture sitting in the heme ring.
Calcium, drawn from bone to bind oxygen inside red cells.
Iron, the mineral hemoglobin uses to transport oxygen in blood.
Vitamin C, treated as if it were the piece of heme that binds oxygen.

explanation: Hemoglobin uses iron to bind and transport oxygen. That is why iron sits in the heme of the red cells that supply working muscle in a race. Sodium, calcium, and vitamin C are not the mineral in that oxygen-carrying site.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses sodium with the mineral in heme. Sodium matters for sweat and fluid, not for hemoglobin's oxygen binding.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses calcium with an oxygen carrier. Calcium is not drawn from bone to bind oxygen inside red blood cells.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses vitamin C with iron. Vitamin C is not the piece of heme that binds oxygen; iron is the mineral hemoglobin uses.

prompt: Before a hot-weather camp, rookies ask the athletic trainer how to set drinking for the week when each session will feel different. What starting plan should the trainer give them?

options.text: Chug a large volume in the final minutes, then stop drinking.
Wait for strong thirst, then copy whatever amount a teammate happens to drink.
Begin the day a little dry so the first session feels lighter.
Begin euhydrated, then adjust drinking from each session's body-mass change.

explanation: The starting plan is to begin euhydrated, then individualize. Pre- and post-session body mass shows how much fluid that athlete lost, so the next bout can be adjusted instead of copied from a teammate. A last-minute chug, thirst alone, or starting dry misses that plan.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a last-minute chug with a hydration plan. Stopping after a large late volume does not replace a euhydrated start adjusted from body-mass change.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses thirst and a teammate's bottle with an individual plan. Sweat losses differ, so drinking should be adjusted from each rookie's own scale change.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a lighter feeling with a smart start. Beginning dry adds a deficit before camp rather than starting euhydrated.

prompt: Forty minutes before a hard interval ride, a cyclist eats a large cheese-and-bacon plate. Why can that very high-fat choice be a problem once the watts climb?

options.text: The fat slows gastric emptying and can leave the stomach upset.
The fat leaves the stomach faster than a lower-fat carbohydrate meal.
The protein in the cheese, not the fat, is what slows the stomach.
The plate is the right fuel choice because these repeats run on fat.

explanation: A very high-fat meal this close to hard riding stays in the stomach. Fat slows gastric emptying, so the cheese-and-bacon plate can cause gastrointestinal discomfort once the watts climb. It does not empty faster than carbohydrate, and fat is not the fuel those intervals need.

distractorExplanations.b: Reverses gastric emptying. A very high-fat plate leaves the stomach more slowly than a lower-fat carbohydrate meal, which is why it bothers the ride.
distractorExplanations.c: Blames the cheese protein for a fat problem. The very high fat content is what slows emptying and can upset the stomach.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses hard intervals with fat-fueled work. The plate is a problem because fat lingers, not because fat is the right fuel for the repeats.

prompt: Halfway through a 90-minute basketball scrimmage, a guard asks how a commercial sports drink differs from the plain water cooler sitting on the sideline?

options.text: It adds creatine, which the plain water cooler does not carry.
It can supply carbohydrate and electrolytes along with the fluid.
It replaces the meals the guard still needs over the rest of the day.
It is flavored water, with no carbohydrate and no electrolytes added.

explanation: In a long, intense scrimmage, a sports drink is not just the water cooler with flavor. It can provide carbohydrate and electrolytes together with fluid, which plain water does not. It does not add creatine, and it does not stand in for the guard's later meals.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a sports drink with a creatine product. The difference from plain water in this scrimmage is carbohydrate and electrolytes, not creatine.
distractorExplanations.c: Overstates the drink. Carbohydrate and electrolytes with fluid do not replace the meals the guard still needs later in the day.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a sports drink with flavored water. The commercial drink can carry carbohydrate and electrolytes that the cooler does not.

prompt: An athlete with celiac disease asks the strength coach to write a therapeutic meal plan for the condition. Who is allowed to provide that medical nutrition therapy?

options.text: The strength coach, working from a generic team meal template.
A teammate who already follows a popular gluten-free eating pattern.
A registered dietitian or another appropriately licensed clinician.
The staff member who orders snacks for trips and home events.

explanation: A therapeutic plan for celiac disease is medical nutrition therapy, not general sports-nutrition education. That work belongs to a registered dietitian or another appropriately licensed clinician. The strength coach should refer rather than write the treatment plan, and a teammate's habit or the snack order is not a license to do it.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses coaching education with treatment. A generic team template does not authorize the strength coach to write medical nutrition therapy.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a personal eating pattern with clinical care. A teammate who avoids gluten is not licensed to treat this athlete's condition.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses food logistics with therapy. Ordering team snacks is not medical nutrition therapy for celiac disease.

prompt: A swimmer reads an olive-oil bottle that assigns the same 4 kilocalories per gram used for protein and asks what a gram of this fat actually yields?

options.text: Keep 4 kilocalories per gram, the figure this label copies from protein.
Each gram of this fat yields about 9 kilocalories, not the label's 4.
Yields nothing, because a bottle of oil is treated as free of energy.
About 4 kilocalories per ounce, which puts the protein figure on the wrong unit.

explanation: Olive oil is fat, and fat yields about 9 kilocalories per gram, not the 4 used for protein and carbohydrate. The bottle copied the protein figure onto a fat. The swimmer should count about 9 per gram and should not treat the oil as energy-free.

distractorExplanations.a: Keeps the label's mistake. Four kilocalories per gram is the protein figure, and this oil is fat at about 9.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats cooking oil as a free food. A gram of fat still supplies about 9 kilocalories, so the bottle is not zero-energy.
distractorExplanations.d: Mixes the unit and the macronutrient. The error is using 4 instead of about 9 per gram, not moving the protein number onto ounces.

prompt: After a night game, a pitcher wants a beer because he heard alcohol refills glycogen. What should the staff tell him about using that drink for recovery?

options.text: Beer deepens sleep, so it belongs in the night recovery routine.
Beer rehydrates him better than a drink that has carbohydrate and sodium.
Alcohol impairs rehydration and sleep and is a poor recovery fuel.
Alcohol should be the main calorie source for restoring glycogen.

explanation: Alcohol is not a recovery fuel. It works against rehydration and impairs sleep, so a postgame beer does not refill the pitcher's glycogen or finish the night's recovery. Carbohydrate and fluid with sodium do that job; alcohol should not be the calorie source aimed at glycogen.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses alcohol's effect on sleep. Beer does not deepen recovery sleep, and it does not earn a place in the postgame routine for that reason.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses beer with a rehydration drink. Alcohol impairs rehydration compared with fluid that supplies carbohydrate and sodium.
distractorExplanations.d: Makes alcohol the glycogen fuel. It is a poor recovery calorie source and should not be what restores glycogen after the game.

prompt: A volleyball libero finishes practice 2 percent lighter on the locker-room scale, feels no thirst, and asks whether replacing that loss can wait?

options.text: Replace the fluid, because a 2 percent loss is meaningful sweat.
Wait for thirst, because a 2 percent drop is too small to replace.
Leave it overnight, because sleep restores that fluid without drinking.
Ignore the scale until cramps have already started in practice.

explanation: A 2 percent body-mass loss after practice is meaningful sweat loss, even though she is not thirsty. Thirst is a poor sole plan, so the fluid should be replaced rather than deferred. Chasing a bigger drop or waiting for cramps leaves that deficit in place.

distractorExplanations.b: Treats 2 percent as trivial and thirst as the trigger. That loss is already enough to replace, and waiting for thirst is not the plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats sleep as a fluid replacement. Rest does not put back a 2 percent sweat loss, so the fluid should be replaced rather than left overnight.
distractorExplanations.d: Waits for cramps before acting on the scale. A 2 percent loss is already a reason to replace fluid, without using cramps as the signal.

prompt: Late in a 100-minute rugby practice, a flanker is fading and wants to know if carbohydrate taken while play continues can spare the glycogen still left in muscle?

options.text: No, carbohydrate during play slows the stomach and should be skipped.
No, glycogen is spared by the meal after practice, not by feeding now.
Yes, but plain water is what spares glycogen, so carbohydrate should stay out of the bottle.
Yes, carbohydrate during this long practice can spare muscle glycogen.

explanation: This practice runs well past about an hour, and the flanker is still playing. Carbohydrate taken during that work can spare the muscle glycogen he has left. Plain water does not provide that fuel, and the post-practice meal is a separate refill, not the only chance to spare glycogen.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats every during-practice carbohydrate feeding as a stomach problem to skip. In a session this long, carbohydrate can spare glycogen while play continues.
distractorExplanations.b: Moves the whole benefit to the meal after practice. Carbohydrate during the second half can spare glycogen before that later meal.
distractorExplanations.c: Gives the sparing role to plain water. Water replaces fluid, but the carbohydrate in the bottle is what can spare muscle glycogen.

prompt: A tired rower asks the coach for an iron pill after a teammate said vitamin C would fix the low energy. What should the coach do?

options.text: Give her the iron pill today, because feeling tired by itself shows an iron need.
Do not hand out a guessed iron dose, and refer the rower instead.
Skip the iron and use vitamin C, because vitamin C replaces iron.
Start both supplements now and leave the referral for later.

explanation: Fatigue is not a reason for the coach to hand out iron. Vitamin C does not stand in for iron, and guessing a dose is outside the coach's scope. The rower should be referred to a qualified clinician rather than started on either supplement from the boathouse.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats tiredness as proof she needs iron. The coach should not give an iron pill on that guess and should refer instead.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses vitamin C with a substitute for iron. Vitamin C does not replace iron, and swapping one pill for the other is still a guess.
distractorExplanations.d: Stacks both products and delays the referral. Starting supplements from the dock is the scope error this situation requires the coach to avoid.

prompt: A hockey club stripped starch from the menu for the week before a weekend tournament, then on opening morning the skaters feel flat. What fueling error is showing up in those repeated hard shifts?

options.text: They ate too much carbohydrate, so the flat start comes from over-fueling.
They drank too much water, and that is what emptied the game-day tank.
The low-carbohydrate week left the repeated shifts under-fueled.
They should have cut protein, because protein is the fuel for those shifts.

explanation: Repeated hard shifts rely on carbohydrate through glycolysis. A week with starch stripped off the menu leaves that work under-fueled, which is why opening morning feels flat. The error is the low-carbohydrate lead-in, not too much carbohydrate, too much water, or a protein cut.

distractorExplanations.a: Reverses the week's menu. They removed starch, so the flat shifts come from too little carbohydrate, not from over-fueling.
distractorExplanations.b: Blames fluid for an empty fuel tank. Extra water did not create this flatness; the low-carbohydrate week did.
distractorExplanations.d: Names the wrong nutrient to cut. Protein is not the fuel for those repeated shifts, and cutting it would not fix a low-carbohydrate week.

prompt: A lacrosse attacker who rarely drinks coffee plans to double her usual mug on game morning. What caffeine decision should the coach give her?

options.text: Check the sport's list and her tolerance, and do not double the mug.
Double the mug, treating a bigger coffee as a free edge on game morning.
Remove coffee, treating caffeine as banned without checking that sport's list.
Ignore tolerance, treating caffeine as if athletes respond in one shared way.

explanation: Caffeine can be a legal aid in many sports, and it becomes a rules problem only when that sport's list says so. The coach should check the list and her own tolerance. Doubling a rare coffee the morning of the game ignores both, and banning it without looking at the list is the other mistake.

distractorExplanations.b: Turns a bigger mug into an automatic edge. Doubling coffee on game morning skips her tolerance and the sport's list.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats caffeine as banned before anyone checks. The decision starts with that sport's list, not a blanket removal.
distractorExplanations.d: Drops individual tolerance. Athletes do not respond alike, so her usual intake matters as much as the rule list.

prompt: Ten minutes before kickoff a fullback tries to chug a gallon of plain water after barely drinking all afternoon. How should the staff correct that last-minute plan?

options.text: Let him finish the gallon so one late chug covers the rest of the game.
Cut off drinking now, treating any fluid before kickoff as the cause of a sloshing stomach.
Switch the gallon for a stimulant and leave sodium out of the plan.
Replace fluid steadily, adding sodium if sweat losses run long.

explanation: The mistake is the last-minute gallon, not fluid itself. A huge chug of plain water sloshes and cannot make up for an afternoon of barely drinking. Replacement should be steady, with sodium when sweat losses are large and long. Hours of water alone can also dilute blood sodium.

distractorExplanations.a: Keeps the chug and calls it a plan. One gallon in the last ten minutes does not steadily replace what he skipped all afternoon.
distractorExplanations.b: Bans fluid because a chug can slosh. The correction is steady replacement, not arriving at kickoff with nothing to drink.
distractorExplanations.c: Swaps water for a stimulant and drops sodium. Long sweaty work needs steady fluid and sodium, not a stimulant in place of the gallon.

prompt: A novice lifter misses the shake he planned for the first half hour after lifting and fears the whole session was wasted. What should the coach tell him?

options.text: The session was wasted because the shake missed that first half hour.
Missing that first half hour does not cancel the training he just did.
He should double tomorrow's protein to repay the missed shake.
A branded powder is required, so a normal meal later in the day cannot support synthesis.

explanation: There is no 30-minute window that erases the session if the shake is late. Missing the first half hour does not cancel the lifting he already did, and muscle-protein synthesis is not reserved for a branded powder. A normal meal later still contributes; doubling tomorrow is not a repayment rule.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the first half hour as an anabolic window that voids the workout. Missing that shake does not waste the session.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents a next-day repayment. Doubling tomorrow's protein is not required to rescue a shake that missed the first half hour.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a product with the process. Synthesis is not limited to a branded powder, and a later meal can still support it.

prompt: A boxer brings a commercial detox tea to make weight overnight and asks the coach to approve it as a cutting method before the morning scale?

options.text: Approve the tea, because it removes fat without hurting performance.
Approve the tea if the label calls the blend plant-based and gentle.
Refuse the tea, because a rapid fluid cut hurts performance.
Keep the tea and skip meals instead, so the overnight scale still moves.

explanation: A detox tea used to make weight overnight is a rapid cut in a different package. The loss is largely fluid, and that kind of drop hurts performance. A plant-based label does not make it a sound method, and pairing the tea with skipped meals keeps the same harm.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats the tea as selective fat loss. An overnight detox cut dumps fluid and hurts performance rather than removing fat cleanly.
distractorExplanations.b: Lets the label approve the method. Plant-based wording does not stop a rapid fluid loss from hurting the next day's performance.
distractorExplanations.d: Keeps the tea and adds missed meals. That is still a rapid cut aimed at the morning scale, with the same cost to performance.

prompt: The strength staff already bought iron bottles after reading a blog about low hemoglobin and is ready to assign an anemia diet. What is the correct professional step?

options.text: Refer to a physician or dietitian rather than assigning that diet.
Hand out the bottles, because the blog already settled the hemoglobin question.
Write the anemia menu, treating that blog as if it were inside coach scope.
Increase the bottles so the staff-written menu can work faster.

explanation: Buying iron and drafting an anemia diet from a hemoglobin blog is the coach practicing medical nutrition care. The professional step is to refer to a physician or dietitian and not assign that diet or distribute the bottles. A blog does not put a treatment menu inside the strength staff's scope.

distractorExplanations.b: Lets a blog authorize the bottles. The staff should refer to a physician or dietitian rather than hand out iron they already purchased.
distractorExplanations.c: Treats the anemia menu as coaching. Writing that diet from a hemoglobin story is outside scope and should be referred.
distractorExplanations.d: Escalates the same error. More bottles do not fix a staff-written anemia plan; the step is to refer instead of prescribing.

prompt: After two bread-free days a climber sees the scale plunge and celebrates fat loss. Which stored partner left with the glycogen to explain that quick change?

options.text: Body fat, because two bread-free days clear fat at that same speed.
Muscle protein, because glycogen and muscle are stored as one unit.
Stored iron, because cutting starch pulls iron out of the body with it.
Water, since glycogen is stored in muscle along with water.

explanation: Glycogen is stored with water. Two bread-free days drop glycogen, and the water stored with it leaves too, so the scale falls fast. That plunge is not the same speed of fat loss, and it is not muscle protein or iron walking out with the glycogen.

distractorExplanations.a: Reads a fast scale drop as fat loss. Two low-carbohydrate days move water that was stored with glycogen, which is quicker than fat loss.
distractorExplanations.b: Pairs glycogen with muscle protein. The partner that leaves with glycogen in this cut is water, not the muscle itself.
distractorExplanations.c: Invents an iron loss to explain the scale. Cutting starch drops glycogen and its water, not stored iron.

prompt: During a set of repeated 30-second hill sprints, a track athlete says fat burning is the main fuel because the session feels aerobic. Which fuel actually dominates those repeats?

options.text: Fat oxidation, the fuel that dominates a long easy aerobic effort.
Carbohydrate, because these 30-second repeats are glycolytic.
Muscle protein, as if the hill repeats ran mainly on amino acids.
Sodium from the bottle, as if that mineral were fueling the sprints.

explanation: Fat oxidation can dominate a long, easy aerobic session. Repeated 30-second hill sprints are glycolytic work, so carbohydrate is the fuel that dominates even if the session feels aerobic to him. Protein and sodium are not the energy source for those repeats.

distractorExplanations.a: Applies the easy-aerobic fuel to 30-second repeats. Fat oxidation fits the long easy session, not these glycolytic hills.
distractorExplanations.c: Names muscle protein as the sprint fuel. Amino acids are not what dominates repeated 30-second efforts.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an electrolyte with a fuel. Sodium in the bottle does not power the hill repeats; carbohydrate does.

prompt: On the morning of a championship, a swimmer orders an unfamiliar spicy bean dish she has never eaten and asks whether that novel choice is safe before the race?

options.text: Yes, a brand-new spicy bean plate is a smart race-morning carbohydrate boost.
Yes, if she adds a heavy pour of oil so the dish empties more slowly.
No, a new spicy high-fiber dish raises gut risk before the race.
No, she should skip every meal and race after a long overnight fast.

explanation: Race morning is a poor time for a food she has never eaten. A new spicy, high-fiber bean dish raises the chance of gastrointestinal trouble before the championship. Adding oil slows emptying further, and skipping every meal is a different mistake, not the fix for this plate.

distractorExplanations.a: Treats a novel spicy bean dish as a clever carbohydrate boost. New high-fiber food on race morning is a gut risk, not a smart trial.
distractorExplanations.b: Adds fat to a dish that is already a problem. Extra oil slows emptying and does not make an unfamiliar spicy plate safe.
distractorExplanations.d: Replaces one error with an overnight fast. She should not debut this dish, and she also should not skip pre-race food entirely.

prompt: A parent tells the coach that creatine is a banned hormone like a steroid and demands it be treated as a stimulant. How should the coach classify the product?

options.text: Treat it as a banned steroid hormone and remove it from the weight room.
Call it a stimulant and raise the serving on the morning of competition.
Let the coach write the loading plan as though it were a prescription he is allowed to sign.
It is not a hormone or a stimulant, and a qualified person sets its use.

explanation: Creatine is not a steroid hormone and it is not a stimulant. The coach should not agree with that classification or pretend to prescribe a loading plan. A qualified person sets the product; the coach's job here is to correct the parent's picture, not to invent a dose or pull it as a banned hormone.

distractorExplanations.a: Accepts the parent's hormone claim. Creatine is not a banned steroid, so removing it on that basis misclassifies the product.
distractorExplanations.b: Calls creatine a stimulant and then increases the serving. It is not a stimulant, and game-morning escalation is the wrong handling.
distractorExplanations.c: Turns a loading plan into a prescription the coach signs. The coach should not pretend to prescribe it; a qualified person sets the product.

prompt: A collegiate soccer midfielder's blank resistance sheet still lists no position demands, no injury history, and no season objective. Staff are about to choose lifts anyway. What has to be settled before any exercise is selected?

options.text: Needs analysis and the training goals, settled before any exercise is chosen
The heaviest squat the facility already owns, written in before any goal is named
Last season's exercise menu, copied forward with the weekdays swapped and the goals unread
A block of isolation work, so the page looks full before goals are set

explanation: Needs analysis and the training goals come before exercise choice. Position demands, injury history, and the season objective tell the staff which qualities this midfielder needs. Picking lifts on a blank sheet skips the step that makes the rest of the program specific.

distractorExplanations.b: Starting from a familiar heavy squat treats equipment habit as the first decision. The midfielder's demands and goals are still unwritten.
distractorExplanations.c: Copying last season's menu skips a fresh look at this player's position, injury history, and current objective.
distractorExplanations.d: Isolation work is an assistance choice later in a session. It does not replace deciding what the program is for.

prompt: A trained discus thrower wants the next mesocycle to emphasize maximal strength rather than muscle size or conditioning. Bar speed on the competition lift still looks sharp. Which loading pattern matches that aim?

options.text: Moderate loads, many repetitions, and very short rests between those sets
Heavy loads, few repetitions, and long rests between those sets
Light loads taken to failure on every set, with almost no recovery between them
Unloaded circuits that keep a heavy barbell out of the training session

explanation: Maximal strength in a trained thrower is stressed with heavy loads, relatively few repetitions, and long rests so each set can still produce high force. Higher-rep short-rest work and unloaded circuits target size, endurance, or a different quality than the one requested.

distractorExplanations.a: Many repetitions and very short rests fit a size or endurance emphasis. They do not match a request for maximal strength.
distractorExplanations.c: Taking light loads to failure with almost no recovery trains a different quality and lets bar speed decay. Maximal strength needs heavy loads and long rests.
distractorExplanations.d: Unloaded circuits remove the heavy loading that maximal strength requires. Keeping the barbell out of the session misses the aim.

prompt: Snatch pulls were placed after a grinding leg-press finisher that left a track jumper's legs shaky. The warmup is already finished and speed on the pull still matters. Where should those power pulls sit in the hour?

options.text: Right after the leg-press finisher, so the tired legs learn to grind the pull
On a later day, after the week's assistance exercises have already been finished
Early, once the warmup is done and before fatiguing assistance work
Dropped in favor of the leg press, since both movements train the lower body

explanation: Power quality depends on speed and technique, both of which fall once assistance work has fatigued the legs. The snatch pulls belong early, after the warmup and before the grinding leg-press finisher, not at the end of the hour when the jumper is already shaky.

distractorExplanations.a: Putting the pulls after the finisher asks for speed from legs that are already shaky. Power work is placed before that fatigue, not used as a grind.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting until every assistance exercise is finished delays the pulls until fatigue is highest. Power lifts go before that work, not after the whole week of it.
distractorExplanations.d: A leg press does not replace a snatch pull. Both can train the lower body, and the power exercise still belongs early in the hour.

prompt: Across one swimming season the staff changes volume and intensity on purpose so fatigue stays manageable and a peak arrives on the championship meet. What should they call that organized change across time?

options.text: One easier week of swimming, with no plan past those few practices
Dropping intensity for the whole season so the swimmer stays on easy distance
Repeating the same set of repeats every week until the meet arrives
Planned variation of training over time to manage fatigue and adaptation

explanation: Periodization is planned variation of training variables over time. The staff are changing volume and intensity on purpose so fatigue stays manageable and the peak lands on the championship meet. That organized change is the definition, not a single easy week or an unchanged weekly repeat.

distractorExplanations.a: One easier week with no plan past it is a short break in stress, not the season-long pattern of planned change described here.
distractorExplanations.b: Dropping intensity for the whole season removes the variation. The staff are changing volume and intensity on purpose, not parking the swimmer on easy distance.
distractorExplanations.c: Repeating the same week until the meet is the absence of planned variation. Periodization is the organized change across the season.

prompt: A novice rower completed every prescribed repetition with clean positions on Tuesday and again on Thursday. Recovery looks ordinary and the bar path stayed consistent. What progression fits that two-for-two result?

options.text: A modest load increase on the next exposure, with technique kept intact
A sharp jump in load plus extra sets added on that same next day
The same load held much longer, because two clean days are not a reason to progress
A switch to a different lift, instead of progressing the one just performed cleanly

explanation: Two consecutive sessions of completing the prescribed repetitions with clean technique earn a modest load increase under the two-for-two rule. The rower's positions stayed consistent and recovery looks ordinary, so the next exposure can take a small load bump while technique is preserved.

distractorExplanations.b: A sharp jump plus extra sets on the same day stacks two progressions at once. The earned step is a modest load increase, not a large combined jump.
distractorExplanations.c: Holding the load much longer ignores two clean sessions. The two-for-two result is a reason for a modest increase, not a reason to freeze the load.
distractorExplanations.d: Switching lifts abandons the pattern that was just performed cleanly. Progression here means a modest load increase on this lift, with technique kept intact.

prompt: Repeated near-max front-squat doubles require the lifter to produce high force on every set. The coach is setting the clock between those efforts. Which rest best supports repeated maximal-strength work?

options.text: A few breaths, so the next double starts again with little recovery
About two to five minutes, scaled to the lift and the lifter
Rest until the next training day, with no further set attempted in this session
