Whatever gap occurs while plates are changed, with no target interval at all

explanation: Repeated maximal-strength sets need enough rest to restore force. About two to five minutes, adjusted for the front squat and this lifter, is the window that supports another high-force double. A few breaths leaves the next set under-recovered, and ending the session is not a between-set rest.

distractorExplanations.a: A few breaths is too short for repeated maximal-strength doubles. Force on the next set drops when recovery is cut to a couple of breaths.
distractorExplanations.c: Waiting until the next day abandons the repeated sets this session is built around. The needed rest is a few minutes between doubles, not the end of the workout.
distractorExplanations.d: An untimed plate change is not a planned rest. Maximal-strength doubles need a target of about two to five minutes so force can return.

prompt: Preacher curls, a bench press, and hang cleans are all on today's sheet, currently listed in that order. Speed and technique on the most demanding lift need protection. Which sequence follows standard resistance-exercise ordering?

options.text: Assistance curls before any multijoint press or power clean on the sheet
The bench press first, with hang cleans saved for the very end of the hour
Power exercises, then other core multijoint lifts, then assistance work
Whichever lift feels easiest to start, with no regard for accumulating fatigue

explanation: Standard ordering puts power exercises first, then other core multijoint lifts, then assistance work. Hang cleans should lead, the bench press follows as the other multijoint lift, and preacher curls come last so fatigue from the curls does not spoil speed on the clean.

distractorExplanations.a: Curls before the press and the clean reverse the order. Assistance work comes after power and other core multijoint lifts, not before them.
distractorExplanations.b: Saving the hang cleans for the end puts the power exercise after the bench. Power leads, then the other multijoint lift, then assistance.
distractorExplanations.d: Starting with whatever feels easiest ignores fatigue. Ordering is power, then other core multijoint work, then assistance, so the most technical lift is still fast.

prompt: A basketball guard just finished a run of demanding weeks, and the next week is written with fewer sets on purpose so stress falls while practice continues. What is that planned reduction?

options.text: An unplanned shutdown because the gym happens to be closed for repairs
The same number of sets as the hard weeks, with the week renamed and the work unchanged
A new all-out test inserted into the middle of the easier week
A planned temporary reduction in training stress while practice continues

explanation: A deload is a planned, temporary cut in training stress. Fewer sets were written on purpose so stress falls while the guard still practices. It is not a building closure, a renamed week that changes nothing, or a week that adds a new all-out test.

distractorExplanations.a: A gym closure is an unplanned stop. A deload is a planned cut in stress, and practice is still supposed to continue.
distractorExplanations.b: Renaming the week without cutting sets does not reduce stress. The deload is the actual reduction, not a new label on the same work.
distractorExplanations.c: An all-out test adds stress in the week that was written to lower it. A deload cuts training stress on purpose.

prompt: Romanian deadlift entries in the log show how many sets were done, how many repetitions each set held, and what weight was on the bar. A coach wants one external-load figure for comparing blocks. How is volume load commonly calculated?

options.text: Sets multiplied by repetitions multiplied by the load on the bar
The heaviest single repetition, ignoring how many sets were completed
The number of sets alone, because repetitions do not enter the figure
Minutes spent in the room divided by how many exercises were listed

explanation: Volume load is a simple external-load total: sets multiplied by repetitions multiplied by the load. The Romanian deadlift log already has those three numbers, so the figure used to compare blocks multiplies all three rather than keeping only the heaviest rep, the set count, or the time in the room.

distractorExplanations.b: The heaviest single repetition ignores how many sets and repetitions were done. Volume load multiplies sets, repetitions, and load together.
distractorExplanations.c: Set count alone drops repetitions and load. Both belong in the product, so the number of sets is not the volume load.
distractorExplanations.d: Session minutes divided by the exercise count is not volume load. The figure comes from sets, repetitions, and the weight on the bar.

prompt: One annual plan shifts volume and intensity across long blocks of the year. A second plan raises and lowers those same variables several times inside a much shorter span. What separates linear periodization from undulating periodization?

options.text: Linear plans freeze the exercise list, while undulating plans change which sport is being played
Linear plans shift volume and intensity across longer phases; undulating plans shift them more often
Linear plans use easy days alone, while undulating plans use heavy days alone across the year
Both labels describe one identical weekly layout and differ by the name printed on the calendar

explanation: Both models organize overload, and they use different time scales. Linear periodization shifts volume and intensity across longer phases. Undulating periodization varies those same variables more often, inside a shorter span. The difference is how frequently the plan changes, not a change of sport or a shared weekly label.

distractorExplanations.a: Neither model is defined by freezing the exercises or by swapping the sport. The split is how often volume and intensity change.
distractorExplanations.c: Neither model is easy-days-only or heavy-days-only. Both use volume and intensity; linear changes them across longer phases and undulating changes them more often.
distractorExplanations.d: The two labels are not the same weekly layout. They differ in how frequently volume and intensity are shifted.

prompt: A volleyball hitter lands quietly, shows the strength base the staff required, and has tolerated the current contacts for a full month. The coach is deciding whether plyometric intensity can rise. When is that step appropriate?

options.text: As soon as the hitter asks for a higher box, even if the landings look shaky
After the championship, regardless of how the current landings already look
After landing control, strength, and tolerance are shown at the current level
At the first session, before control or tolerance at this level has been seen

explanation: Plyometric intensity progresses only after the athlete shows landing control, the required strength, and tolerance at the current level. This hitter lands quietly, has the strength base, and has tolerated the contacts for a month, so a rise in intensity is appropriate now. Asking for a higher box, or jumping the step at the first session, skips that check.

distractorExplanations.a: A request for a higher box does not replace the check. Progression waits on landing control, strength, and tolerance, including when the athlete asks early.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting for the championship ignores landings that are already quiet and tolerated. The gate is control, strength, and tolerance at the current level, not the calendar of the meet.
distractorExplanations.d: The first session is too soon if control and tolerance have not been seen. Intensity rises after those are demonstrated, not before.

prompt: Days before a conference final, the sprint group needs to arrive fresh without giving up the fitness already built. Practice time will shrink on purpose. What is that pre-competition taper for?

options.text: Raising volume in the final days so fitness is built at the last minute
Stripping out the fast runs and leaving easy jogging until the final
Inserting a surprise all-out trial so the group can prove it is ready
Cutting fatigue while fitness and event-specific readiness stay in place

explanation: A taper before a major competition cuts fatigue while fitness and event-specific readiness are maintained. Shrinking practice time in the days before the conference final is for that purpose. Building a last-minute volume peak, dropping all fast running, or adding a surprise trial fights the point of the taper.

distractorExplanations.a: Raising volume in the final days adds fatigue when the taper is supposed to remove it. Fitness is already built and should be kept, not reconstructed at the last minute.
distractorExplanations.b: Easy jogging alone can let event-specific readiness slip. A taper cuts fatigue while fitness and sprint readiness stay in place.
distractorExplanations.c: A surprise all-out trial puts fatigue back in. The taper's purpose is to arrive fresh with fitness maintained, not to prove readiness with a new test.

prompt: A rugby forward's size block is being programmed for muscle growth, separate from the heavy-single pattern used when maximal strength is the target. Weekly work and proximity to failure are the open choices. Which feature matters most for hypertrophy?

options.text: Enough weekly volume, with sets taken near enough to failure to recruit fibers
Very heavy singles, long rests, and little weekly set volume on the main lifts
Unloaded mobility, on the view that hard sets are optional for muscle growth
Stopping every set far short of failure so fewer fibers have to be recruited

explanation: Hypertrophy depends on enough weekly volume and on sets taken near enough to failure to recruit fibers. The rugby forward's size block needs that feature. Heavy singles with little weekly volume, unloaded mobility, or stopping far from failure are different targets and do not supply the hard-set volume muscle growth uses.

distractorExplanations.b: Very heavy singles with long rests and little weekly volume fit maximal strength. Hypertrophy needs enough weekly volume with sets near enough to failure.
distractorExplanations.c: Unloaded mobility does not replace hard sets. Muscle growth here depends on weekly volume taken near enough to failure to recruit fibers.
distractorExplanations.d: Stopping far short of failure leaves fibers unrecruited. Hypertrophy sets need to get near enough to failure, alongside enough weekly volume.

prompt: Field-hockey match sprints are short, and the recoveries between them are brief. Conditioning should prepare that pattern and still fit the rest of the training week. How should those intervals be chosen?

options.text: Use long steady runs, treating field sports as one shared energy problem
Match the sport's work-to-rest and energy demand inside the full training week
Copy a bodybuilding rest pattern and ignore how the match sprints are timed
Place the hardest repeats after a grinding lift, once the legs are already spent

explanation: Conditioning for a repeated-sprint sport should match that sport's work-to-rest pattern and energy demand, and it still has to fit the rest of the week. Short hockey sprints with brief recoveries are the pattern to copy. Long steady runs, a bodybuilding rest scheme, or sprints after a grinding lift prepare something else.

distractorExplanations.a: Long steady runs do not match short sprints separated by brief recoveries. The intervals should follow the match's work-to-rest, not a single shared endurance pattern.
distractorExplanations.c: A bodybuilding rest pattern ignores the match. Conditioning is chosen by the sport's work-to-rest and energy demand, then fitted into the week.
distractorExplanations.d: Putting the hardest repeats after a grinding lift trains tired legs, not the match pattern. The intervals still need to match the sport's work and rest inside the week.

prompt: Several weeks of slower swim times, a darker mood, and muscle soreness that does not clear between practices have piled up. The staff must pick the next programming step. What response fits that picture?

options.text: Add another hard week, reading the slump as proof the swimmer is underloaded
Leave the stress unchanged and rename the week as though the work were easier
Cut training stress and check recovery before any further progression
Open a competition taper even though no meet is sitting on the calendar

explanation: Several weeks of falling performance, a darker mood, and soreness that does not clear point to accumulated fatigue. The programming response is to cut training stress and check recovery before progression resumes. Adding another hard week, relabeling an unchanged week, or opening a taper with no meet does not answer that picture.

distractorExplanations.a: Another hard week treats the slump as underloading. Weeks of slower times plus uncleared soreness call for less stress and a recovery check, not more overload.
distractorExplanations.b: Renaming the week without cutting stress changes nothing. The response is an actual reduction plus a look at recovery before progression starts again.
distractorExplanations.d: A competition taper is for a meet, and none is on the calendar. This picture needs stress cut and recovery checked, not a pre-meet sharpening.

prompt: Depth-jump landings show the forward's knees collapsing inward the moment the feet hit. Contacts at this box height are not stable. What should happen to the jump height?

options.text: Lower the box until the landing stays aligned
Raise the box so the inward collapse is practiced under a harder landing
Keep this height and add a weight vest so the forward is forced to stick the landing
Leave the height alone and still count every collapsed contact toward the daily total

explanation: A depth-jump landing that collapses the knees inward is not a landing to progress. The box height should come down until the feet hit with the knees staying aligned. Raising the box, adding a vest, or counting collapsed contacts trains the fault instead of regressing it.

distractorExplanations.b: A higher box makes the unstable landing harder. Valgus on contact is a reason to lower the height, not to practice the collapse from higher up.
distractorExplanations.c: A weight vest at the same height adds load to a landing that is already collapsing. The height should be regressed until alignment holds.
distractorExplanations.d: Counting collapsed contacts keeps the faulty landing in the session total. The height comes down until the landing stays aligned.

prompt: The lumbar spine rounds as soon as the bar leaves the floor on a conventional deadlift. Repetitions are still left on the card. What should happen to this set?

options.text: Finish the remaining repetitions so the written tonnage for the day is still reached
Encourage a deeper round so the lower back is stretched while the bar is moving
Stop the set and reduce the load
Bounce the plates off the floor harder so the next pull looks smoother off the ground

explanation: When the lumbar spine rounds as the bar leaves the floor, the set stops and the load comes down. Finishing the remaining repetitions to protect a tonnage number asks the lifter to pull with a rounded back. A deeper round or a harder bounce does not fix the position.

distractorExplanations.a: Finishing the reps to hit the day's tonnage keeps a rounded lumbar spine under load. The set stops and the load is reduced instead.
distractorExplanations.b: A deeper round increases the fault. Rounding under the bar is a reason to stop and lighten the pull, not a stretch to chase.
distractorExplanations.d: Bouncing the plates changes the start, not the rounded lumbar position. The set should stop and the load should come down.

prompt: Power cleans are written after lunges taken all the way to failure. Bar speed on the clean is this weightlifter's priority. What change belongs on that card?

options.text: Leave the cleans last so the lunges can pre-fatigue the legs on purpose
Replace the cleans with still more lunges to failure and drop the pull from the day
Keep the written order and coach the lifter to grind each clean slowly
Move the cleans ahead of the lunges

explanation: Power cleans were written after lunges taken to failure, which spends the legs before the lift that needs bar speed. The card should move the cleans ahead of those lunges. Leaving them last, replacing them, or turning them into a slow grind keeps technique behind fatigue.

distractorExplanations.a: Pre-fatiguing the legs with lunges to failure is the problem on the card. The cleans move ahead of the lunges so bar speed is still available.
distractorExplanations.b: Dropping the clean for more lunges removes the priority lift. The change is to reorder, with cleans before the lunges, not to delete the pull.
distractorExplanations.c: Grinding the cleans slowly accepts the bad order. Technique-first means moving the cleans ahead of the lunges, not coaching a slow pull at the end.

prompt: Sprint posture breaks on a later repeat, and the coach is pushing the run the way a hypertrophy set is pushed toward failure. Quality was the point of this speed work. What should the coach do?

options.text: Continue until posture collapses, the same way a muscle-growth set is taken to failure
Stop the sprint once quality decays
Add further repeats at the moment the running mechanics start to fall apart
Turn the remainder of the session into an all-out conditioning finish

explanation: Speed work is not programmed to failure the way a hypertrophy set is. Once sprint posture breaks, rep quality has decayed and the repeat should stop. Continuing to collapse, adding repeats as mechanics fail, or converting the session into a conditioning finish trains the breakdown.

distractorExplanations.a: Taking a sprint to postural collapse copies a hypertrophy set. Speed work stops when quality decays, rather than being pushed to failure.
distractorExplanations.c: Adding repeats as mechanics fall apart extends the faulty runs. The sprint stops once quality decays.
distractorExplanations.d: An all-out conditioning finish abandons the speed goal. The session was for quality reps, and those stop when posture breaks.

prompt: Two clean sessions just earned a novice a modest load increase under the two-for-two rule. The same day, the coach also wants to double the number of sets. Which change should be made?

options.text: Add load or add a set, not both
Raise the load and double the sets in that same session
Skip the earned load change and add a second full day of the same work instead
Leave the load and the sets unchanged, treating two clean sessions as too small a sample to progress

explanation: The novice earned a modest two-for-two load increase. The same day should not also double the sets. Add load or add a set, not both. Raising the load and the set count together overshoots that step, and leaving both unchanged ignores the two clean sessions.

distractorExplanations.b: Raising the load and doubling the sets in one session stacks both changes. The earned step is one of them, not both on the same day.
distractorExplanations.c: Adding a second full day skips the progression that was earned and changes the weekly schedule instead. The choice is a modest load or a set, not a new day in place of both.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaving the load and the sets unchanged treats two clean sessions as too little to act on. The earned step is one change, a modest load or a set, not a freeze and not both at once.

prompt: Heavy squats already fill Thursday, and Friday was just filled with a high number of depth jumps. The athlete's knees are the tissue at risk. How should those two stressors be arranged?

options.text: Stack both stressors on Friday so the knees face the squat and the jumps in a single day
Move the depth jumps to the end of Thursday's heavy squat session
Separate the heavy squats from the depth-jump volume
Keep both days as written and rely on a longer warmup to protect the knees

explanation: A heavy squat day and a high-volume depth-jump day should not be stacked when the knees are the tissue at risk. Those stressors are separated. Putting the jumps at the end of the squat session, combining both on Friday, or trusting a longer warmup while the two days stay stacked leaves the same joints under both loads.

distractorExplanations.a: Stacking squats and depth jumps on Friday combines both knee stressors in one day. They should be separated, not piled onto the same date.
distractorExplanations.b: Depth jumps at the end of the heavy squat session are still the same day as the squats. The two stressors need to be separated.
distractorExplanations.d: A longer warmup does not unstack a heavy squat day and a high-volume depth-jump day. The arrangement that protects the knees is to separate them.

prompt: Ten-second sprints are supposed to stay fast and alactic. The card prescribes a one-to-one rest, ten seconds of recovery after each sprint. What rest does this quality session need?

options.text: The one-to-one rest already written, because equal work and rest is what keeps these sprints fast
An even shorter rest, so the repeats shift into a conditioning piece on purpose
No timed rest at all, with the sprints joined into one continuous run
A longer rest that keeps each sprint fast

explanation: Alactic repeats need a rest long enough that the next sprint stays fast. A one-to-one rest on ten-second sprints starts the next effort before that quality returns and turns the session into conditioning. The quality session needs the longer rest, not a shorter one and not a continuous run.

distractorExplanations.a: A one-to-one rest on these ten-second sprints does not keep them fast. Equal work and rest turns the repeats into conditioning, so the rest needs to be longer.
distractorExplanations.b: A shorter rest pushes the session further toward conditioning. Quality alactic repeats need more rest, not less, so each sprint can stay fast.
distractorExplanations.c: Joining the sprints into one continuous run removes the rest that keeps each rep fast. The session needs a longer rest between sprints.

prompt: Reconditioning is underway, and someone wants the old pre-injury maximum tested this week. Clearance paperwork lists firm limits on load and range. What should the program follow?

options.text: The pre-injury maximum, tested this week to see what strength remains
The limits written in the medical clearance
Whatever load the athlete feels ready to try, including loads past the written limits
A record attempt this week, treating reconditioning as the time to peak

explanation: An athlete in reconditioning does not get the pre-injury maximum tested that week. The program follows the load and range limits in the medical clearance. Testing the old max, going by feel past those limits, or attempting a record treats clearance as optional.

distractorExplanations.a: Testing the pre-injury maximum this week ignores the clearance limits. Reconditioning follows those limits rather than rechecking the old max.
distractorExplanations.c: Feel is not a substitute for the written limits. Loads past clearance are outside the program that should be followed this week.
distractorExplanations.d: A record attempt peaks the week instead of respecting clearance. Reconditioning follows the medical limits, not a new max.

prompt: A spring road race is the only competition on a marathoner's calendar, yet the whole plan is a powerlifting peaking block. The race demands were never used to pick the method. What should drive the plan?

options.text: The road race, not a powerlifting peak
The powerlifting peak, because a squat max is the method that prepares this marathon
Whichever method the platform schedule happens to make convenient during that month
A bodybuilding split, because the race date does not change how the strength work is organized

explanation: Specificity follows the competition. This marathoner's only event is a spring road race, so that race drives the method. A powerlifting peaking block as the whole plan prepares a different contest. Facility convenience and a bodybuilding split also ignore the race that is actually on the calendar.

distractorExplanations.b: A powerlifting peak prepares a maximal squat, not a road race. The competition on the calendar is the marathon, and that event should drive the plan.
distractorExplanations.c: Platform convenience is a scheduling constraint, not the competition demand. The road race, not the room's calendar, picks the method.
distractorExplanations.d: A bodybuilding split organizes work around size. The race date does change the method, and the road race is what the plan should follow.

prompt: Barbell curls were written ahead of every clean because someone wanted the arms warmed with isolation work first. The clean is the priority lift of the day. How should those two be ordered?

options.text: Curls first, so the arms are pumped before the clean begins
Curls alone, with the clean removed from the day entirely
Clean first, curls after
Alternate single curls and single cleans until both lists are finished

explanation: Assistance work does not come before the clean. Curls were written first to warm the arms, but the clean is the priority lift and should be done first, with curls after. Pumping the arms beforehand, dropping the clean, or alternating the two puts isolation ahead of the lift that needs to stay sharp.

distractorExplanations.a: A pump from curls before the clean is the order that was written, and it puts assistance first. The clean comes first and the curls follow.
distractorExplanations.b: Removing the clean leaves only the assistance exercise. The fix is to reorder, not to drop the priority lift.
distractorExplanations.d: Alternating curls and cleans still inserts isolation before later cleans. The clean is completed first, and the curls come after.

prompt: Thirty seconds between heavy deadlift doubles has killed bar speed by the third set. Maximal strength is the goal printed on the card. Why is that rest the wrong tool for this goal?

options.text: Thirty seconds is the rest maximal strength needs, so the slowdown must have a different cause
The bar slowed because the load is too light, so the rest should get even shorter next time
Short rest is what maximal strength wants, because each double should turn into a grind
Thirty seconds fits a different goal than maximal strength

explanation: Thirty seconds between heavy doubles fits a different goal than maximal strength. Bar speed died by the third set because the rest was too short to support repeated high-force efforts. Maximal strength is not served by calling that interval correct, by shortening it further, or by turning the doubles into a grind.

distractorExplanations.a: Thirty seconds is not the rest maximal strength needs between heavy doubles. The slowdown is what that short rest produces, not a mystery with another cause.
distractorExplanations.b: Blaming a too-light load and shortening the rest further misses the goal. The rest is already too short for maximal strength, which is why bar speed died.
distractorExplanations.c: A grind is not the aim of maximal-strength doubles. Short rest fits a different goal; maximal strength needs the bar to stay fast across sets.

prompt: Volume is falling before a championship, but a new max-out was added to test readiness. Some intensity on ordinary heavy work was supposed to stay. What does a sound taper do in this spot?

options.text: Add the max-out and also raise volume so readiness is proven while fatigue is still high
Cut volume, keep some intensity, and skip the max test
Drop the volume and the heavy repetitions, then test a max during meet week
Keep the max-out, because a taper is unfinished until a new record has been attempted

explanation: A taper cuts volume and keeps some intensity so fatigue falls and fitness stays. Adding a new max-out to test readiness puts fatigue back. The sound choice is to cut volume, keep some intensity on the ordinary heavy work, and skip the max test rather than raising volume or dropping every heavy repetition.

distractorExplanations.a: Adding a max-out and raising volume puts fatigue back into the taper. Volume should fall, some intensity should stay, and the max test should be skipped.
distractorExplanations.c: Dropping the heavy repetitions removes the intensity a taper keeps. The max during meet week also puts a test back in. Cut volume, keep some intensity, and do not test a max.
distractorExplanations.d: A taper is not unfinished without a record attempt. The max-out adds fatigue. Volume comes down, some intensity stays, and the test is left out.

prompt: Four sets of five repetitions at one hundred kilograms are logged on the bar. The coach expects that volume-load figure to fall if sets are cut even though the load stays. What is the volume load of the original four sets?

options.text: 2,000 kilograms
20 kilograms
400 kilograms (4 × 100)
100 kilograms, using the bar weight alone

explanation: Volume load is sets times repetitions times load. Four sets times five repetitions times one hundred kilograms is 2,000 kilograms. Cutting sets lowers that total even when the bar weight stays at one hundred kilograms. Twenty kilograms drops the load, and four hundred kilograms is sets times load with the five repetitions left out.

distractorExplanations.b: Twenty kilograms is four times five, sets times repetitions, with the one-hundred-kilogram load never multiplied in.
distractorExplanations.c: Four hundred kilograms is 4 × 100, sets times load, with the five repetitions left out of the product.
distractorExplanations.d: One hundred kilograms is the bar weight alone. Volume load still multiplies that load by the four sets and the five repetitions.

prompt: Tuesday is heavy and Friday of the same week is a moderate day on the same lower-body lifts. Volume and intensity both change inside that single week. Which periodization model is that weekly pattern?

options.text: Linear, because any load change inside a week counts as one of the long blocks
A deload, because Friday is lighter than Tuesday and the week therefore counts as a planned cut
Undulating, because the heavy day and the moderate day share one week
A taper, because two different loading days mean the competitive season is already ending

explanation: Undulating periodization puts the heavy day and the lighter day inside the same week. Tuesday heavy and Friday moderate, with volume and intensity both changing in that week, is that model. It is not a long linear block, not a deload just because Friday is lighter, and not a taper signaling the end of the season.

distractorExplanations.a: A within-week swing is not a long linear block. Linear plans shift volume and intensity across longer phases. Heavy Tuesday and moderate Friday in one week is undulating.
distractorExplanations.b: A lighter Friday is not automatically a deload. The week still contains a heavy day and a moderate day, which is undulating variation, not a planned cut of the whole week.
distractorExplanations.d: Two different days do not mean the season is ending. A taper is a pre-competition reduction in fatigue. This week is undulating because the heavy and moderate days share it.

prompt: Agility footwork shares a day with the beep test. The card puts the footwork after the test, when the athletes are gassed, even though the skill itself is the point. When should that footwork be coached?

options.text: After the beep test, so fatigue makes the footwork feel more like a tired match
On the day after the beep test, rather than while movement is still sharp
Left off the card because a conditioning test is also scheduled that day
While movement quality is still high

explanation: Agility footwork is a skill and should be coached while the athletes can still move well. Placing it after the beep test, when they are gassed, practices the pattern in a fatigued state. The footwork belongs earlier, while movement quality is still high, not the next day by rule and not deleted because a test shares the date.

distractorExplanations.b: Moving footwork to the day after the test still refuses to coach it fresh. The skill belongs while movement quality is high, which on this day is before the athletes are gassed.
distractorExplanations.a: Coaching footwork after the beep test puts skill work behind fatigue. A tired-match feeling is a different goal. This footwork should be done while movement quality is still high.
distractorExplanations.c: Sharing the day with a conditioning test is not a reason to drop the footwork. It is a reason to place the skill while the athletes can still move well.

prompt: A collegiate lineman is unracking a heavy bench press, and the next attempts are loaded even heavier. Where should the spotters stand, and when are extra spotters required?

options.text: Stand at the head of the bench with hands ready, and add spotters when the load is very heavy.
Stand at the lifter's feet so the bar path can be watched without reaching toward the bar.
Grip the bar for every repetition so the lineman does not have to hold the full load.
Wait outside the rack and step in after a repetition has already failed.

explanation: On the bench press the primary spotter stands at the head of the bench with hands ready near the bar, so a liftoff and a missed rep can both be assisted. When the load is very heavy, more spotters are added rather than leaving one person to catch the whole bar. Watching from the feet, carrying every rep, or walking in after the miss leaves the bar unsupported at the moment it fails.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a viewing spot at the feet with the bench-press spot. From the feet the hands cannot reach the bar; the spotter belongs at the head.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses spotting with lifting the set for the athlete. A spotter assists the liftoff and a failed rep and does not hold the full load on every repetition.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a late rescue with a set spot. Extra spotters are already in place for a very heavy attempt, not summoned after the rep has failed.

prompt: Two Olympic racks are being bolted into a crowded weight room, and the installer asks how far apart the bar ends must sit. What clearance should the staff require between those bars?

options.text: Crowd the sleeves together so one more rack fits, even if a spotter cannot stand between the bars.
Leave the clearance the facility standard needs for loading, spotting, and walking past.
Measure the gap from the uprights and ignore how far the loaded sleeves project into the aisle.
Keep a path behind the lifter and let the bar ends overlap the next station.

explanation: Bar spacing follows the facility standard, not a single gap invented to fit more racks. The ends need enough room to load plates, to spot, and to walk past a moving bar. Measuring only the uprights, overlapping the next station, or crowding the sleeves removes one of those three working spaces.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses floor capacity with safe spacing. Fitting another rack by crowding the sleeves leaves no room to spot or to pass a loaded bar.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the upright-to-upright gap with the space the loaded sleeves actually occupy. Plates stick out, and that projection is part of the clearance.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a path behind the lifter with clearance at the bar ends. Overlapping the next station blocks loading and puts a passer in the bar's path.

prompt: Midway through conditioning, a soccer goalkeeper collapses beside the goal and does not answer. Staff have a written emergency plan they have practiced. What is their first action?

options.text: Clear the remaining cones so the field is tidy before anyone calls for help.
Wait for the head athletic trainer to walk over before treating the collapse as an emergency.
Recognize the collapse as an emergency and activate the rehearsed plan for this facility.
Carry the goalkeeper into the hallway before deciding whether the written plan applies.

explanation: The first step is to recognize the collapse as an emergency and activate the plan this staff already rehearsed for this facility. That plan is what assigns roles, communication, and how help is reached. Tidying the field, waiting for one person to arrive, or moving the goalkeeper before the plan starts delays the response the rehearsal was built for.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses scene cleanup with the first emergency step. Cones can wait; the rehearsed plan starts as soon as the collapse is recognized.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses waiting for a particular clinician with activating the plan. Recognition does not pause until the head athletic trainer happens to arrive.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses moving the athlete with the first action. Carrying the goalkeeper off before the plan is activated skips the rehearsed sequence.

prompt: Loose anchor bolts are found on a power rack before the first group trains. The director asks why that finding still has to be written down. What does the inspection record accomplish?

options.text: A signature lets the next shift skip looking, because yesterday's check still covers the rack.
The log itself puts a damaged rack back in use, because the signature completes the repair.
It names the coach on duty so a later complaint has someone to blame.
The record shows the loose bolts were found and that staff addressed them.

explanation: The inspection record shows that the loose anchor bolts were identified and that staff did something about them. That written trail is what later maintenance and accountability rely on. A signature does not excuse the next shift from looking, it does not repair the rack, and it is not a list of whom to blame.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a logged check with permission to skip the next one. The record documents this finding; it does not retire future inspections.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses paperwork with the repair. Writing down the loose bolts does not tighten them or return the rack to service.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses documentation with assigning blame. The record shows the loose bolts were found and addressed, not which coach to fault later.

prompt: A rowing club is hiring the person who will supervise evening lifting for its scholarship athletes. Which qualifications must that supervisor bring to the floor?

options.text: A current certification for this role, CPR and AED skill, and work that stays inside scope.
Years of personal lifting and a weekend course, with CPR treated as optional.
Any teammate who can demonstrate the day's lifts may supervise without a certification.
A CSCS used to diagnose injuries on the floor, with emergency skills left to the trainer.

explanation: The person supervising scholarship athletes needs a current certification appropriate to the role, current CPR and AED competence, and the limit of staying inside that scope. Years on the platform or a weekend course do not replace the credential or CPR. Holding a CSCS does not add the authority to diagnose injuries.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses lifting experience and a short course with the required credential. Personal mileage does not replace a current certification or CPR and AED skill.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the ability to demonstrate a lift with qualification to supervise. A teammate who can perform the work is not the credentialed supervisor.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a CSCS with a license to diagnose, and it drops CPR and AED skill. The credential is used inside scope, and emergency competence stays with the supervisor.

prompt: A sprinter clutches the left side of his chest and stops mid-stride on the indoor track. Nearby staff are running that session. How should they respond to that pain?

options.text: Treat the tightness as normal for sprints and have him finish the repetition.
Stop the exercise, activate the emergency plan, and obtain medical help.
Lower the intensity and complete the remaining reps so the session still counts.
Stretch the chest and rerun the sprint before medical help is called.

explanation: Chest pain during the sprint is a reason to stop the exercise, activate the emergency plan, and obtain medical help. It is not managed by finishing the rep, cutting the pace, or stretching and then repeating the sprint. Those choices keep a possible medical emergency inside the workout.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses chest pain with ordinary sprint tightness. Finishing the repetition skips the stop, the emergency plan, and medical help.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a lighter workout with a response to chest pain. Dropping the intensity and completing reps still continues exercise instead of getting medical help.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a stretch-and-retest with emergency care. Rerunning the sprint before help is called delays the plan the pain requires.

prompt: Before a freshman class runs a repeated sprint battery, staff hand each runner a consent packet. What must that packet explain if the consent is actually informed?

options.text: The sprint names and a clause that waives the staff's duty of care.
A captain's spoken go-ahead, so a written packet is unnecessary for this class.
The procedures, the risks, the benefits, and the runner's right to decline or stop.
A coach-signed waiver that takes away the runner's right to quit mid-battery.

explanation: Informed consent for the sprint battery explains the procedures, the risks, the benefits, and the runner's right to decline or stop. A list of test names plus a waiver of duty, a captain's verbal go-ahead, or a form that removes the right to quit does not give the runner that choice.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a name list and a duty waiver with informed consent. Naming the sprints and waiving care leaves out risks, benefits, and the right to stop.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a teammate's spoken approval with the runner's own informed consent. A captain cannot replace the written explanation of procedures, risks, and benefits.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a waiver that strips the right to quit with consent. Informed consent preserves the right to decline or stop; it does not sign that right away.

prompt: Unsupervised alumni keep walking into the varsity weight room while teams are training. Why does this floor need written access and supervision rules?

options.text: Regulars already know who belongs, so a slogan on the door replaces a written rule.
The coach who arrives first can set access that day, so a standing policy is unnecessary.
The sheet lists equipment brands in the room and does not need to say who may enter.
They state who may train, what supervision is required, and what conduct is expected.

explanation: Written access and supervision rules state who may train, what oversight that training requires, and what conduct is expected on the floor. A door slogan, a decision made by whoever arrives first, or a list of equipment brands does not set those duties, so unsupervised alumni keep walking in.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a familiar slogan with a written rule. People who already train here are not the policy that tells alumni whether they may enter.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses daily improvisation with a supervision rule. Access set by the first coach to arrive changes every day and never states the required oversight.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses an equipment inventory with an access policy. Brand names on a sheet do not say who may train or what supervision is required.

prompt: Broken strands are visible on the cable of a seated-row machine, and athletes are lined up to use that station. What is the correct way to handle the machine?

options.text: Remove it from service until a qualified repair is finished and the machine is inspected.
Tape the fray and allow experienced lifters to finish the week on a lighter stack.
Set a lower pin so the damaged section travels less, and leave the station open.
Keep it available unless an athlete has already been hurt by that cable.

explanation: A cable with broken strands can fail under load. The seated row comes out of service and stays out until a qualified repair is finished and the machine is inspected. Tape, a lighter stack, or waiting until someone is already hurt leaves the line of athletes on a foreseeable failure.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a tape wrap and a lighter stack with a repair. Experienced lifters are not a substitute for taking the machine out of service until it is repaired and inspected.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a shorter travel path with a sound cable. A lower pin still loads the broken strands, so the station does not stay open.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a response after an injury with removing a known hazard. The cable comes out of service when the strands are seen, not after an athlete is hurt.

prompt: A testing morning includes a beep test, flying sprints, skinfolds, a maximal squat, push-up endurance, a pro-agility run, and a power clean. In what order should that battery be run?

options.text: Run the beep test first so later power scores come from athletes who are already tired.
Nonfatiguing measures, then agility, power and strength, sprints, local endurance, then the aerobic test.
Maximal squat and power clean before the skinfolds, then the sprints, and agility after that.
Flying sprints first, the beep test second, and the skinfolds once everyone is fatigued.

explanation: Fatigue changes later scores, so the battery runs from least fatiguing to most. Skinfolds come first, then the pro-agility run, then the power clean and maximal squat, then the flying sprints, then push-up endurance, and the beep test last. Starting with the beep test, the max squat, or the sprints contaminates the measures that should still be fresh.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a fatigued score with a valid power score. The aerobic beep test is last so it does not tire athletes before power and strength.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses maximal strength with a nonfatiguing measure. The squat and power clean come after skinfolds and agility, not before the skinfolds.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses sprints and the beep test with the start of the battery. Sprints follow power and strength, the beep test is last, and skinfolds stay first.

prompt: The same standing broad-jump protocol is repeated a week later with the same cues, surface, and warm-up. Which property is the staff checking when the scores stay consistent?

options.text: Validity, meaning a matched score proves the jump measured aerobic fitness.
Protocol flexibility, meaning a different surface next week would still be the same test.
Reliability, meaning consistent scores when the same protocol is repeated.
Difficulty, meaning the test is sound when athletes cannot match their first score.

explanation: Reliability is the property on display when the broad jump produces consistent scores under the same cues, surface, and warm-up. Matching numbers do not prove the jump measured some other quality, such as aerobic fitness. Changing the surface, or treating a failure to match as the goal, abandons the repeated protocol that reliability requires.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses reliability with validity. Consistent broad-jump scores do not prove the test measured aerobic fitness; they show the protocol repeated cleanly.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a stable protocol with freedom to change the setup. A different surface next week is a different test, not evidence of reliability.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses difficulty with reliability. Reliability is agreement across repeated trials, not a pattern of athletes missing their first score.

prompt: Performance and medical files for a national-team lifter are kept in a shared office that several departments use. Which practice protects that lifter's confidentiality?

options.text: Post the latest scores on the office door so every department can follow progress.
Email the full file to every assistant who entered the building that day.
Leave the folder open on the platform desk so notes can be added between sessions.
Limit the files to authorized people and use secure storage and communication.

explanation: Confidentiality limits the lifter's performance and medical files to authorized people and requires secure storage and communication. A door posting, a wide email to everyone who badged in, or an open folder on the platform desk lets unauthorized departments read the file.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses convenient sharing with confidentiality. Scores on the office door are visible to every department, not only to authorized people.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses building access with authorization to see the file. An assistant who entered that day is not automatically allowed to receive the medical record.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses easy note-taking with secure storage. An open folder on the platform desk is neither limited nor secure between sessions.

prompt: Teammates start shoving one another and swinging a loaded barbell between sets on the platform. Why do facility rules ban that horseplay?

options.text: Uncontrolled play around a moving bar can injure people, and that risk is preventable.
The rule is about keeping music off, and the loaded bar is not the danger.
Shoving is acceptable once every bar is back on a rack, because a stored bar is harmless.
Joking with a bar is a coaching cue, and the ban applies to visitors rather than athletes.

explanation: Horseplay is banned because the barbell and the plates are moving. Shoving and swinging that bar on the platform can injure the teammates and anyone nearby, and that injury is preventable. The rule is about the loads. It still applies between sets, and it applies to the athletes themselves.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a music preference with the horseplay ban. The danger is the moving loaded bar, not whether music is playing.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a racked bar with a bar that is being swung. The ban exists because loads move; storing them later does not make the swinging safe now.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a coaching cue with uncontrolled play, and it limits the ban to visitors. Athletes swinging a loaded bar are the hazard the rule targets.

prompt: A volleyball attacker asks the strength staff to name the tissue causing her ankle pain and to say how many weeks she will miss. What should the staff do?

options.text: Name the ligament and set the weeks she will miss if she accepts that label.
Refer her to an appropriately licensed clinician for that diagnosis.
Tape the ankle and clear her when a body-weight squat no longer hurts.
Make the diagnosis on site because no athletic trainer is in the building today.

explanation: Naming the tissue and setting the weeks missed is a diagnosis. Strength staff do not make that diagnosis; they refer the attacker to an appropriately licensed clinician. Her agreement, a tape job that feels better, or the absence of a trainer does not move diagnosis into the coach's scope.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the athlete's agreement with a license to diagnose. Naming the ligament and the weeks missed is the clinical decision the staff must refer.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a tape job and a pain-free squat with a diagnosis and a clearance. Symptom relief during a body-weight squat does not identify the tissue or the timeline.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses an empty training room with expanded scope. No athletic trainer on site is a reason to refer, not a reason to diagnose the ankle there.

prompt: A Saturday booking places a large field-hockey roster into one weight room with too few racks and one qualified supervisor. What must the schedule respect?

options.text: Book every player who is free that hour, and add racks if someone later complains.
Give the room to the biggest roster each week, whatever the racks and staffing.
Fit the group to the space, the racks, and the number of qualified staff.
Skip the headcount when the work is mobility and the bars stay on the racks.

explanation: A safe schedule fits the field-hockey group to the room, the racks on hand, and how many qualified people can supervise. Booking everyone who is free, favoring the biggest roster, or ignoring headcount because the bars stay racked leaves athletes unwatched in a space that cannot hold the session.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an open invitation with a schedule that fits the room. Adding racks after a complaint does not match the group to today's space, equipment, and supervisor.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses roster size with a right to the floor. The biggest group still has to fit the racks and the qualified staff on duty.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses unloaded bars with no need for supervision. Mobility in a crowded room still has to match the space and the number of qualified staff.

prompt: A strength coach keeps a vertical-jump series because the scores repeat, then labels that series as the squad's aerobic-fitness test. What is wrong with that label?

options.text: Stable scores prove the series measures aerobic capacity and can be used to rank the squad on fitness.
A jump that repeats cleanly still does not measure aerobic fitness.
Once a test repeats, it measures whatever quality the coach writes on the data sheet.
Heavy breathing after the jumps converts the series into an aerobic measure.

explanation: The vertical jump can be reliable and still not valid for aerobic fitness. Reliability means the scores repeat when the protocol stays the same. Validity asks whether the test measures the quality being claimed. A jump that is stable week to week remains a power measure, so the aerobic label is the mistake.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a consistent score with proof of the named quality. Repetition supports reliability and does not turn the jump into an aerobic-capacity test.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses the coach's label with validity. Writing aerobic fitness on the sheet does not change what a repeated vertical jump measures.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses being winded with aerobic fitness. Heavy breathing after jumps does not make the series a measure of aerobic capacity.

prompt: An emergency binder has sat unopened on an office shelf since it was printed in August, and nobody has walked through the pages. What do the staff still need to do?

options.text: Count the unread binder as complete because it was printed and placed on the shelf in August.
Wait for a real incident, then practice whichever step failed during that event.
Leave the binder closed unless an outside reviewer asks to see that a document exists.
Walk through the written plan with the staff before a real emergency.

explanation: A binder nobody has practiced is not an emergency plan in action. Staff still need to rehearse the written steps with the people who would run them, before an athlete is actually down. Printing the pages, waiting for the first incident, or opening the binder for a reviewer leaves the response unrehearsed.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a printed document with a rehearsed plan. A binder on the shelf since August has not been walked through, so it is not ready.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses the first real incident with the rehearsal. Practice happens before someone is hurt, not as a review of the step that already failed.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses showing a document to a reviewer with preparing the staff. An unopened binder satisfies neither the rehearsal nor a real response.

prompt: A forward's knee is swollen, and the coach holds a pen over the blank that would mark the forward cleared for Saturday. What should the coach do with that sheet?

options.text: Leave the knee uncleared and refer the forward to a licensed clinician.
Write cleared for Saturday when the swelling looks mild and the forward wants to play.
Clear the knee for the match and note that a clinician can look at it next week.
Mark the forward cleared if a sideline jog produces no visible limp.

explanation: Writing cleared on the Saturday sheet is a participation decision the coach is not licensed to make. The swollen knee stays uncleared and the forward is referred to a licensed clinician. Mild swelling, the wish to play, a review delayed until next week, or a jog without a limp does not authorize that clearance.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a mild look and the athlete's wish to play with medical clearance. The coach does not write cleared on the basis of how the swelling appears.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a delayed clinical visit with clearance now. Noting that a clinician can look next week still marks the knee cleared for the match.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a jog without a limp with a clinician's clearance. A sideline functional check is not the referral, and it does not fill in the Saturday blank.

prompt: During a heavy clean, the platform door is unlocked and a visiting parent steps onto the lifting surface as the bar leaves the floor. What should access control require here?

options.text: Allow the parent to watch from the lifting surface if they stay quiet while the bar is moving.
Treat the open door as acceptable when a coach is somewhere else in the building.
Stop the parent; access rules keep non-participants off the platform.
Finish the clean, then decide whether the parent may remain beside the bar.

explanation: Access rules keep people who are not in the session off the platform while a bar is moving. An unlocked door does not give the parent permission to step onto the lifting surface. Quiet watching from inside the platform, a coach elsewhere in the building, or finishing the clean first all leave a bystander in the bar's path.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a quiet bystander with an allowed position. Staying silent on the lifting surface still puts the parent where the bar is moving.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a coach somewhere in the building with access control at the platform. An open door during the clean is not permission to enter.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses finishing the lift with controlling access. The parent is already on the surface as the bar leaves the floor, so the decision cannot wait until the clean ends.

prompt: A fire alarm sounds while a deadlift is locked out, and the lifter asks to finish the pull so the bar can be put away. What should the lifters do under the facility's written plan?

options.text: Take one more repetition so the bar is stored, then walk toward the exit.
Leave the racks immediately and do not finish the deadlift.
Wait under the roof until the alarm stops, and resume if nobody calls it a real fire.
Keep the bar in hand when the alarm is a familiar sound, and leave if smoke appears.

explanation: The facility's written plan says to evacuate, so the lifters leave the racks immediately and do not finish the deadlift. Another repetition, waiting out the alarm, or staying because no smoke is visible yet contradicts that plan. The alarm is the cue to go.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses storing the bar with following the evacuation plan. One more repetition keeps the lifters at the rack after the plan has said to leave.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses waiting to see if the alarm is real with evacuating. The written plan says to leave the racks at once, not to resume if the alarm stops.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses visible smoke with the cue to leave. A familiar alarm still means evacuate; the plan does not wait for smoke.

prompt: A barbell sleeve is visibly bent. A staff member wipes the chalk off that bar and starts to roll it back toward the next group. What should happen to the bar?

options.text: Wiping the chalk off counts as the inspection, so the bar returns to the next group.
A slight bend stays in service when experienced lifters are the ones who use that bar.
Turn the bent sleeve away from the lifter and leave the bar in the rotation.
Take the bent bar out of service until it is repaired and inspected.

explanation: Wiping chalk off a bar is cleaning, not an inspection, and a bent sleeve is damage. The bar comes out of use until it is repaired and inspected again. A small bend, a rotated sleeve, or a limit to experienced lifters still puts a damaged bar back under load for the next group.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses cleaning chalk off the bar with inspecting it. A wipe does not clear a bent sleeve, and the bar does not return to the next group.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a small bend and an experienced user with a sound bar. The sleeve is still bent, so the bar stays out of use until it is repaired and inspected.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses hiding the bend with removing it. Turning the sleeve away leaves the damaged bar in the rotation.

prompt: Beep-test results from the morning battery are about to be pasted into the roster's group message so every player sees every score. Who may receive those results?

options.text: The sport coach who is already authorized to receive those results.
Every player on the roster, because they trained together and already know who was slow.
The group message now, with the scores deleted from the thread the next morning.
Any assistant who asks, because a group message is quicker than opening a private file.

explanation: The beep-test results go to the sport coach who is already authorized to receive them, not into a group message the whole roster can read. Training in the same session, deleting the thread the next morning, or saving time for an assistant does not authorize that wider disclosure.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses sharing a session with permission to see every score. Teammates who trained together are not the authorized recipient of the battery results.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses deleting a message later with keeping the results confidential. The roster has already seen every score once the group message is sent.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses speed with authorization. An assistant who asks, and a faster group message, do not replace the sport coach named to receive the results.

prompt: The floor policy's supervision limit is already exceeded, with two qualified coaches present and forty athletes training. What adjustment does that written limit require?

options.text: Keep all forty athletes, since two coaches can see the whole floor from the center.
Count an unqualified intern toward the limit and leave all forty athletes in the room.
Shrink the group or add a qualified coach so the written limit holds.
Set the written limit aside for veterans who have trained in this room before.

explanation: The policy already states a supervision limit, and two qualified coaches with forty athletes are past it. Staff either shrink the group or add another qualified coach until that written limit holds. Watching from the center, counting an unqualified intern, or skipping the limit for veterans ignores the ratio the policy wrote down.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a sight line from the center with the written supervision limit. Seeing the floor does not bring forty athletes back inside a limit two coaches have already passed.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses an unqualified intern with a qualified coach. The intern does not count toward the limit, and the headcount stays over the policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses experience in the room with an exemption. Veterans do not set the written limit aside for this session.

prompt: On a heavy back squat, the person assigned to spot stands in front of the lifter with arms crossed, watching depth. Where does that spotter need to be instead?

options.text: In front with arms crossed, so depth can be judged without the spotter touching the bar too early.
Behind the lifter, close enough to catch the bar if the squat fails.
Across the room, stepping closer after the lifter calls for help.
At the lifter's toes, holding the plates so the descent can be steered from the front.

explanation: A back-squat spotter has to be where the bar can be caught if the lifter misses. Standing in front with arms crossed cannot do that. The working places are behind the lifter, or at the ends of the bar when the load needs more than one person. Watching depth from the front is a coaching view, not a spot.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a view of depth with a spot. Arms crossed in front leave the spotter unable to catch the bar when the squat fails.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a distant coach with a spotter in position. Stepping in after the lifter calls is too late to catch a bar that is already failing.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses steering the plates from the toes with catching the bar. The front of the lifter is the wrong place, and holding the plates there is not the spot.

prompt: The defibrillator sits in a closet behind a locked office, while this room's emergency plan puts the unit on the wall beside the platform. What should staff do with it?

options.text: Leave it in the locked closet so the unit is harder for someone to take.
Move it into a desk drawer that the head coach keeps locked between sessions.
Keep the closet location if the office key hangs on a hook the closing staff can find.
On the wall beside the platform, where the written plan places it.

explanation: The emergency plan names the wall beside the platform, so that is where the defibrillator has to be. A locked office closet, a private desk drawer, or a key on a hook may slow theft and still hide the unit from the person who needs it when someone collapses. Staff follow the location the plan already set.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses theft protection with the planned location. A locked closet keeps the defibrillator away from the platform wall where the plan says it belongs.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a locked drawer with the place named in the plan. The head coach's desk is not the wall beside the platform.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses knowing where the key hangs with having the unit where the plan places it. A findable key does not move the defibrillator onto the platform wall.

prompt: A new intern offers to run the full testing battery alone while the CSCS leaves for a scheduling meeting down the hall. What supervision does the battery require?

options.text: A CSCS stays in the room; the intern is not the supervisor.
The intern may run every station alone after watching the battery one time last week.
Holding the clipboard makes the intern the qualified supervisor for the morning.
The CSCS may leave after the opening test if the protocol sheet is posted on the wall.

explanation: The testing battery is supervised by a qualified professional, and a new intern is not that supervisor. The CSCS stays in the room. One prior observation, a clipboard, or a protocol sheet on the wall does not replace the person responsible for the session.

distractorExplanations.b: Confuses watching the battery once with being qualified to run it. The intern still does not supervise the morning alone while the CSCS is in a meeting.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses holding the clipboard with the qualified supervisor role. The paper does not make the intern the person responsible for the battery.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a posted protocol with supervision in the room. The CSCS does not leave after the first test; the sheet on the wall is not a supervisor.

prompt: A hamstring strain happens on the final sprint, and a staff member produces the consent form and asks for a signature. When should that form have been signed?

options.text: After the strain, so the signature records the injury that just happened on the sprint.
At cool-down, because a nod before the sprints already settled the consent question.
Before the first test, while the athlete can still decline.
When someone is hurt; a battery in which nobody is injured does not need the form.

explanation: Informed consent is signed before any test starts, so the athlete can still decline the procedures, the risks, and the right to stop. Producing the form after the hamstring strain, at cool-down, or only when someone is hurt is too late. The signature authorizes participation in advance; it does not document the injury.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses an injury report with informed consent. Signing after the hamstring strain records nothing the athlete agreed to before the sprint; the form was already due.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses a nod and a cool-down signature with consent obtained in advance. The form is signed before the battery begins, not after the last sprint.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses consent with an incident form. The battery needs the signature whether or not anyone is hurt, and it needs it before testing starts.

prompt: A rack upright cracks after the break. Two coaches insist the morning walk-through was enough because both of them remember looking at that rack. What does that account leave out?

options.text: The morning memory is the record, and a written line would duplicate that look.
A written inspection record; remembering the look does not document it.
Two coaches remembering the same look counts as documentation when they agree today.
A written log starts when equipment fails, not when a morning check looked acceptable.

explanation: An inspection that lives only in memory was not documented. After the upright cracks, two coaches remembering the morning look still leaves no written record of the check. Agreement between them is still memory, and a log is not reserved for the day something breaks.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses memory of the morning look with an inspection record. Remembering the check does not document it, and writing it down is the record, not a duplicate.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses two matching memories with documentation. Agreement today still leaves the morning check unwritten.
distractorExplanations.d: Confuses a failure report with the inspection record. The log covers the check itself, including a morning look that seemed acceptable, not only the moment the upright cracks.

prompt: In the lobby, a proud parent asks staff to place a youth lifter's testing numbers on the public team website before tonight's post. What must staff have before posting?

options.text: Nothing further; the parent asked in person and looked pleased, so the post can go up tonight.
The parent's spoken request, which publishes a minor's scores once it is said aloud in the lobby.
A note in the team chat, after which the public website post is already authorized.
The authorization the facility policy names for releasing those numbers.

explanation: Youth testing numbers stay off the public website until staff have the authorization the policy names. A parent who seems proud in the lobby, a request spoken aloud, or a note in the team chat is not that authorization. Enthusiasm does not publish the child's scores.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a proud in-person request with authorization. Looking pleased in the lobby does not meet the permission the policy names before a public post.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses saying the request aloud with the authorization required for a minor's scores. A spoken ask in the lobby is not the policy's named permission.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a team-chat note with the authorization to publish. Messaging the team does not clear the numbers for the public website.

prompt: A prowler sled is parked across the marked fire exit, and the coach says it will sit there for just this hour as the group walks in. What has to happen before training starts?

options.text: Leave the sled for the hour and send the group through a different door.
Keep the sled in the exit through the heavy work and move it when the session ends.
Leave it blocking the exit and assign someone to move it if an alarm sounds.
Move the sled so the marked fire exit is clear before training.

explanation: The marked fire exit has to be clear before anyone trains. Parking the prowler sled across it for just this hour blocks egress for the whole session. Another door, a plan to slide the sled when the session ends, or moving it only if an alarm sounds leaves the exit blocked while the group is inside.

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses a different door with a clear fire exit. Sending the group elsewhere does not unblock the marked exit the sled is covering.
distractorExplanations.b: Confuses moving the sled at the end with clearing it before training. The exit stays blocked through the heavy work, which is when people would need it.
distractorExplanations.c: Confuses a person assigned to react to an alarm with an exit that is already clear. The sled has to be moved before the session, not after an alarm starts.
